title: The Governed Analytics Platform
text:
Welcome
This tutorial takes you from “I have some comma-separated values (CSV) and Excel files” to “I run a governed analytics platform that an organisation trusts with its decisions.” It is built around one architecture, shown above. You build every layer yourself, with real data, on a laptop, using free tools. You then learn to deploy the same pattern in human resources (HR), education, supply chain, retail, oil and gas, power, banking, pensions and telecoms.

title: The Governed Analytics Platform
text:
The four levels


🟢 Level 1 · NoviceChapters 1–4. See the whole system. Read files of every shape. Profile data and find what’s wrong with it.


🔵 Level 2 · PractitionerChapters 5–9. SQL. Bronze, silver, gold. Dimensional modelling. Data tests and the publish gate.


🟣 Level 3 · AdvancedChapters 10–13. The semantic layer. Vector search and artificial intelligence (AI). Serving to SQLite, PostgreSQL and Dataverse. Shiny dashboards.


⚫ Level 4 · MasterChapters 14–16. Orchestration and monitoring. Security and privacy. Deploying in an organisation and growing it.


The sector playbooks (Chapters 17–25) apply the whole architecture to one industry each, using a runnable pipeline. The capstone (Chapter 26) is where you prove mastery.
Ready to build one for your own organisation? Appendix F — DIY prompt book: from your raw data to a live dashboard is a hands-on prompt book with a downloadable starter kit. It takes you from raw files, databases and application programming interfaces (APIs) to a live, tested, scheduled dashboard in fourteen stages, with a practice organisation to rehearse on first.

title: The Governed Analytics Platform
text:
How every chapter works
Each chapter follows the same rhythm:

What · Why · When · Who. A four-line orientation, so you know where the chapter sits in the architecture before you start.
Concepts. Plain-English explanation with a business example.
🧠 Prompts. The exact prompt that produced each block of code. Paste it into Claude, Positron Assistant or Copilot, compare what you get with the reviewed version here, and notice the differences. You are the reviewer. The AI is the junior analyst.
Code you run. Every code block in this book is executed when the book is built. If you can read it here, it works.
🏋️ Exercises in three tiers: 🟢 warm-up (10 min), 🟡 core (30 min), 🔴 stretch (open-ended). Solutions are folded underneath. Try first.
✅ Mastery check. Questions you should be able to answer aloud, without notes, before moving on. Model answers are folded underneath, as with the exercises: answer first, then compare.
🏢 In the organisation. What this layer looks like in a real company: who owns it, what goes wrong, what it costs.

title: The Governed Analytics Platform
text:
The running example
The main thread of the book is Trans-Sahel Distribution, an fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) distributor with 12 depots, 40 stock-keeping units (SKUs) and two years of weekly sell-out data. The data is synthetic but deliberately realistic, and it contains the problems real data has:

duplicate rows
stockouts recorded as blanks
a depot listed twice under two names
an Excel “board pack” built for printing, not analysis

You will find every one of them, fix it in the right layer, and prove the fix with a test.

title: The Governed Analytics Platform
text:
What you need

A laptop (Windows, macOS or Linux) with R ≥ 4.3, Quarto ≥ 1.5 and Positron or RStudio
About 2 gigabytes (GB) of free disk space
No server, no cloud account and no licence. Everything runs locally on DuckDB. Chapter 16 covers when and how to move to the cloud.







The platform you are learning to build is running next door




Open the dashboard: the serving layer of this architecture, live on the course data.
Open the build notebook: every database, step by step, with its prompts.
Platform home: the Shiny edition, the source code and the deployment notes.



The book’s code lives in the mastery/ folder of the Shiny Dashboard Lab. The shared functions are in R/kit.R (the platform kit) and R/retail.R (the running example as a production script). The data is in ../data/raw/.


22 data files available in /home/claude/shiny-dashboard-lab/data/raw 


ab_test_checkout.csv · b2b_funnel.csv · bank_customers.csv · board_pack.xlsx · customer_reviews_labelled.csv · customer_reviews.csv · energy_lab_qc.csv · energy_production_daily.csv · energy_wells.csv · fmcg_depots.csv · fmcg_products.csv · fmcg_sell_out.csv · fmcg_weekly.parquet · hr_attrition.csv · marketing_spend.csv · ng_macro_monthly.csv · pension_complaints.csv · pension_employers.csv · pension_remittances.csv · regional_report.xlsx · retail_basket_sizes.csv · supply_chain_pos.csv








A note on the data



All datasets are synthetic, built for teaching. Where a chapter cites a regulation (NDPA 2023, the Pension Reform Act 2014, Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC) tariff bands, Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC) quality-of-service rules), it describes the principle. Always check the current text of the regulation before relying on a threshold in production.

title: 1  The architecture, end to end
text:
1.1 The problem it solves
🟢 Novice Read this chapter before touching code. Return to it whenever you feel lost.
Picture a Monday executive meeting. Sales says Q3 revenue was ₦6.2bn. Finance says ₦5.9bn. The regional manager’s spreadsheet says ₦6.4bn. Forty minutes go on arguing about whose number is right instead of what to do about it.
Nobody is lying. Each number came from a different file, cleaned differently, with a different idea of what “revenue” includes. The architecture in this book exists to make that meeting impossible. It does three things:

6

Quarto + Shiny, SQLite, PostgreSQL, Dataverse, Power BI

⬇

Keeping it running, safe and lawful

cron/GitHub Actions, Git, .Renviron/Key Vault, Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) data protection impact assessment (DPIA)
It works on Tuesday and nobody knows why it broke on Wednesday




1.2.1 The medallion inside the warehouse
The warehouse has three zones. The names come from Databricks, and they are now standard across Microsoft Fabric, Snowflake and dbt. Think of a cocoa supply chain:

Bronze is cocoa at the farm gate: exactly as it arrived, including the stones and the wet beans. You never throw bronze away, because it is your evidence. Every column is still text, and every row carries its source file and load time.
Silver is cocoa sorted, dried and graded: data types fixed, duplicates removed, codes conformed (one supplier, one code), and history kept. Silver answers “what is true?”
Gold is chocolate on the shelf: tables shaped for decisions. Facts and dimensions (star schemas) and business marts. Gold answers “what do we decide on?”

The rule: each layer reads only from the layer to its left. Gold never reads bronze, and dashboards never read silver.


1.2.2 The gate
The gate is the most important box on the diagram, and the one most often missing in organisations. It is a set of automated tests:

Is the key unique?
Does every sale point to a real depot?
Is the data fresh?
Does it reconcile to Finance’s report?

Pass: the new gold tables are published. Fail: nothing is published, people are alerted, and yesterday’s good version stays live.


1.2.3 Govern: one definition, findable data, grounded AI

The semantic layer is a file of named metrics (revenue = SUM(revenue_ngn), gross_margin_pct = …), each with an owner. Every dashboard, report and AI query compiles its Structured Query Language (SQL) from it.
The vector index stores embeddings (numeric fingerprints of meaning) for text such as complaints and reviews. That makes “find complaints like this one” and retrieval-augmented AI possible.
The catalogue records what each table is, who owns it, where it came from (lineage), whether it holds personal data, and how its tests went.



1.2.4 Serve: meet people where they work
There is no single best output. Choose by audience:








Audience / need
Serve via
Why




Executives exploring KPIs
Quarto + Shiny dashboard
Interactive, governed, branded, free


Finance team in Excel or Power BI
SQLite serving mart or Parquet
One portable file; opens anywhere, offline


Several apps or users writing and reading at once
PostgreSQL
A real multi-user server with permissions


Microsoft-first organisation, Power Apps and Automate
Microsoft Dataverse
Native to Power Platform, with security roles


“Ask a question in English”
AI assistant over the semantic layer
Text-to-SQL that can only use governed metrics


Regulators and the board
Quarto Portable Document Format (PDF) report
Reproducible and signed off





1.2.5 Write-back: the one loop allowed
Data flows one way. When a business user needs to enter data (targets, corrections, survey answers), they do it in an app on PostgreSQL or Dataverse. That app then becomes a source on the next run. Nobody edits the warehouse directly. That one rule keeps lineage intact.

1.3 Why this design and not another?






🧠 Prompt 1.1 — critique an architecture




Here is a draft data architecture diagram [attach image]. Act as a principal data architect reviewing it for a mid-sized Nigerian company. List every problem you see: direction of data flow, layers that are skipped, mislabelled components, missing governance or operations concerns, and anything that would break in production. For each, say why it matters and give the fix. Then propose an improved layered architecture.



The architecture was refined by critiquing an earlier draft (Figure 1.2). The draft got a lot right. It used clean swim-lanes, placed SQLite downstream as a serving copy, and treated PostgreSQL and Dataverse as publish targets. Reviewing it is the first exercise.

section: 1.4 Right-sizing: when not to build all of this
text:
1.4 Right-sizing: when not to build all of this
Architecture is a cost. Match it to your maturity:








Maturity
Symptoms
Build




0 · Ad hoc
One analyst, one spreadsheet, monthly
Nothing yet. Use a tidy Excel template and a Quarto report


1 · Repeatable
Same report rebuilt by hand every month
Bronze + silver + one gold table, scheduled (Chapters 6–8, 14)


2 · Governed
Several teams argue about numbers
Add the gate, the semantic layer and the catalogue (Chapters 9–10)


3 · Shared
Many tools, apps and users need the data
Add serving targets, access control and continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) (Chapters 12, 15, 16)


4 · Enterprise
Terabytes, real time, hundreds of users
Graduate the engine (Fabric, Snowflake, Databricks). Keep the same design



Graduation triggers. Move off a laptop DuckDB when any one of these is true:

the data is over about 100 gigabytes (GB);
more than about 20 people need to write at the same time;
data must refresh in minutes rather than daily;
auditors require centrally managed identity and access.

title: 1  The architecture, end to end
text:
1.5 🏋️ Exercises
E1.1 🟢 Find the faults. Study Figure 1.2. List at least six problems with it, and for each one say which layer of Figure 1.1 fixes it.
E1.2 🟡 Map your organisation. Draw your own organisation’s data flow on one page, using the six layers. For each layer, name the real system (or “missing”). Circle the layer whose absence costs the most, and estimate the cost in hours per month.
E1.3 🔴 Make the case. Write a 300-word memo to your chief financial officer (CFO) arguing for (or against) building levels 1–2 of the maturity table this quarter. Include one risk of building it and one risk of not building it.






Solutions





E1.1. The draft has eight faults:

Two-way arrows everywhere. Data should flow one way. Two-way arrows imply write-back and destroy lineage. Fix: one-way arrows; write-back goes through a source system.
Harvard Dataverse feeds SQLite directly. That skips landing, cleaning and tests. Fix: every source enters through ingest and bronze.
A duplicate “public research data” box with no arrow. Fix: remove it, or connect it through ingest.
“SQLite … optimized for business intelligence (BI)” is mislabelled. DuckDB is the columnar analytics engine; SQLite’s value is portability. Fix: label it “portable serving mart”.
Governance boxes wired one-to-one to arbitrary consumers. Fix: the tests become a gate before publishing; the semantic layer fronts every consumer.
No bronze/silver/gold inside the warehouse. “Clean, transform, model” can’t be tested as one blob. Fix: name the three layers.
No operations and security plane (scheduling, secrets, logs, access, NDPA). Fix: add the plane underneath.
PostgreSQL and Dataverse shown only as serving targets. They are often sources too. Fix: show both roles, linked by the write-back loop.

Minor: the typo “emmeddings”.
E1.2 / E1.3. These are open-ended. A strong answer quantifies the cost of the status quo. For example, 3 analysts × 2 days a month reconciling numbers ≈ 72 person-days a year.

title: 1  The architecture, end to end
text:
1.6 ✅ Mastery check

Explain in two sentences why data flows only one way.
What is the difference between silver and gold? Give one table that belongs in each.
What happens when the gate fails, and why is “keep yesterday’s version live” better than “publish with a warning”?
Name the serving target you would choose for (a) a finance team in Excel, and (b) a Power Apps field app, and say why.








Solutions






One-way flow. Each layer reads only from the layer to its left, so every number in a dashboard can be traced back through gold, silver and bronze to the file it came from. If people could write back into the warehouse, that lineage would break, and nobody could say which version of a number is true. Data entry happens in an app (on PostgreSQL or Dataverse) that becomes a source on the next run.
Silver vs gold. Silver answers “what is true?”: typed, de-duplicated, conformed, with history (e.g. silver.sell_out, silver.depot_history). Gold answers “what do we decide on?”: tables shaped for decisions, such as star schemas and marts (e.g. gold.fct_sales, gold.mart_depot_month).
When the gate fails, nothing is published, people are alerted, and yesterday’s good version stays live. A warning on a published number is ignored the moment it reaches a slide or a board pack. A stale but correct number is labelled with its date; a wrong number does damage and destroys trust in the whole platform.
Serving targets. (a) Finance in Excel: the SQLite serving mart (or Parquet), one portable file Excel reads through Open Database Connectivity (ODBC), offline. (b) A Power Apps field app: Microsoft Dataverse, which is native to the Power Platform and has security roles.

title: 1  The architecture, end to end
text:
1.7 🏢 In the organisation
The architecture is a contract between three groups:

Business owners agree the definitions in the semantic layer.
The data team guarantees the gate.
IT guarantees the plane.

Most failed analytics programmes in Nigerian organisations did not fail on technology. They failed because nobody owned the definition of a metric, or because nothing stopped a wrong file from reaching the board pack. Start every project by naming the owner of each gold table.

title: 2  Your workbench
text:
2.2 A project layout that scales
Use one folder per platform, and the same layout every time:
my-platform/
├── config.yml           ← WHERE things are (paths, servers, schedules). Safe to share.
├── .Renviron            ← WHO you are (passwords, API keys). NEVER shared or committed.
├── .gitignore           ← lists .Renviron, data/db/, *.duckdb
├── R/                   ← reusable functions (kit.R, pipelines)
├── semantic/            ← metrics.yml — business definitions
├── data/raw/            ← sources exactly as received (read-only by convention)
├── data/db/             ← generated databases (rebuildable, so not backed up)
├── notebooks/*.qmd      ← exploration and teaching
├── dashboard.qmd        ← the Shiny dashboard
└── refresh.R            ← the scheduled pipeline
Three rules:

Raw is read-only. Never edit a source file by hand. Fixes go into silver, as code.
Generated means disposable. You must be able to delete data/db/ and rebuild it with one command.
Config is not secrets. config.yml says where; .Renviron says who.

🧠 Prompt 2.2 — hello, DuckDB

  FROM read_csv_auto('%s')

Why DuckDB as the warehouse?




It is free and has no server. It runs inside R or Python, so there is nothing to install or administer.
It is columnar. Aggregating 100 million rows on a laptop takes seconds.
It reads CSV, Parquet, JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) and Excel directly, and talks to PostgreSQL, SQLite and S3.
It speaks standard SQL, so the skills transfer to Snowflake, BigQuery and Fabric.
It graduates without a rewrite: MotherDuck is DuckDB in the cloud.

title: 2  Your workbench
text:
2.7 ✅ Mastery check

What goes in config.yml, and what goes in .Renviron?
Why can DuckDB query a CSV “without importing it”?
Name three things that must never be committed to Git.








Solutions






config.yml says where: paths, server names, schedules, refresh intervals. It is safe to share and commit. .Renviron says who: passwords, application programming interface (API) keys, client secrets. It is never shared or committed.
DuckDB reads the file in place. Its CSV reader scans the file at query time, works out the columns and types, and only reads the columns the query needs, so there is no separate load step.
Never commit: .Renviron (secrets), data/db/ and any *.duckdb file (generated data, an NDPA risk once in Git history), and raw personal data files. Commit code, configuration and definitions instead.

text:
3.8 ✅ Mastery check

Why does bronze read CSVs as text?
Name four things in a “presentation” spreadsheet that must be removed before analysis.
Why is Parquet faster for analytics than CSV?








Solutions






So bronze never loses information. Type guessing turns a value like "12O" (letter O) into a silent NA. Kept as text, it survives, so silver can find it, flag it and fix it with a documented rule.
Any four of: title rows above the header; merged cells (e.g. a region typed once per block); subtotal and “All depots” total rows; footnotes; numbers stored as text with currency symbols and commas ("₦149,023,348"); one column per month (wide, not tidy); hidden sheets.
Parquet is columnar, typed and compressed. A query reads only the columns it needs, types don’t have to be guessed every time, and files are far smaller than the same data as CSV.

3.9 🏢 In the organisation
The cheapest data-quality fix is upstream. Once you have tidied a monthly Excel report twice, meet its author. Agree a data contract: a fixed template, no merged cells, no totals, Unicode Transformation Format, 8-bit (UTF-8), and named on a schedule. One meeting saves twelve months of cleaning code.

text:
4.4 A profile you can re-use






🧠 Prompt 4.3 — a reusable profiler




Write an R function profile_table(con, source_sql) that returns one row per column: type, % null, distinct count, min, max, and the three most frequent values. Run it on hr_attrition.csv.




profile_table <- function(con, src) {
  cols <- dbGetQuery(con, paste("DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM", src))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(cols)), function(i) {
    c <- cols$column_name[i]
    s <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf('SELECT round(100.0*AVG(("%s" IS NULL)::INT),1) pct_null, COUNT(DISTINCT "%s") n_distinct,
                                         MIN("%s")::VARCHAR mn, MAX("%s")::VARCHAR mx FROM %s', c, c, c, c, src))
    top <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf('SELECT "%s"::VARCHAR v FROM %s GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 3', c, src))$v
    data.frame(column = c, type = cols$column_type[i], s, top_values = paste(top, collapse = " | "))
  }))
}

title: 4  Profile before you trust
text:
4.7 ✅ Mastery check

Name the six quality dimensions, with one test each.
What is target leakage, and what question exposes it?
Why does excluding open complaints bias the average resolution time?








Solutions






Completeness (units_sold IS NULL), uniqueness (duplicate week × depot × SKU), validity (uptime_hrs between 0 and 24), consistency (received_date ≥ po_date; every SKU exists in the product master), timeliness (latest week no more than 21 days old) and accuracy (reconciles to Finance’s report within 1%).
Target leakage is a predictor that is only known after the outcome happens, like exit_interview_booked for attrition. It makes a model look brilliant in testing and useless in production. The question that exposes it: “Could I have known this value at the moment I need to make the prediction?”
Open complaints have no resolution time yet, and they are usually the slowest ones. Averaging only the closed complaints leaves out the hardest cases, so the average looks better than reality. This is called right-censoring. Report both numbers, or use survival analysis.

5.3 Combining: JOINs
A join answers “for each row here, find the matching row(s) there.” Four types matter:








Join
Keeps
Business use




INNER JOIN
only matches
facts that have a valid dimension


LEFT JOIN
all left rows, matched or not
“all depots, with sales if any”


ANTI JOIN / NOT EXISTS
left rows with no match
orphans and data-quality checks


FULL JOIN
everything from both sides
reconciliation between two sources




-- Reconcile the Excel regional report to the warehouse, depot by depot (FULL JOIN shows gaps on both sides)
WITH xl AS (SELECT depot_name, SUM(revenue_ngn) AS excel_ngn FROM silver.regional_report GROUP BY 1),
     wh AS (SELECT d.depot_name, SUM(f.revenue_ngn) AS warehouse_ngn
            FROM gold.fct_sales f JOIN silver.depot_history d
              ON f.depot_code = d.depot_code AND d.version = 1
            WHERE year(f.week_starting) = 2025 GROUP BY 1)
SELECT COALESCE(xl.depot_name, wh.depot_name) AS depot,
       round(excel_ngn / 1e6, 1)     AS excel_m,
       round(warehouse_ngn / 1e6, 1) AS warehouse_m,
       round(100 * (excel_ngn / warehouse_ngn - 1), 2) AS gap_pct
FROM xl FULL JOIN wh ON xl.depot_name = wh.depot_name
ORDER BY abs(gap_pct) DESC NULLS FIRST

title: 5  SQL: the language of the warehouse
text:
5.9 ✅ Mastery check

When do you use HAVING rather than WHERE?
What does QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY t DESC) = 1 do?
Why is “average of ratios” usually wrong for margin?








Solutions






WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. “Depots with revenue over ₦1bn” needs HAVING SUM(revenue_ngn) > 1e9.
It keeps one row per key k: the latest by t. Rows are numbered within each k, newest first, and only number 1 survives. It is the standard way to de-duplicate or take the current version.
Averaging ratios gives every row the same weight, so a tiny depot counts as much as Lagos Mainland. Margin must be sum first, divide last: SUM(gross_profit) / SUM(revenue).

Make SQL review part of the culture. No query feeds a board number without a second pair of eyes, and AI-written SQL gets the same review as a junior analyst’s. Keep a shared, Git-versioned folder of “certified queries”. Over time it becomes the seed of your semantic layer.

6.1 Bronze rules
🔵 Practitioner
crumbs: 6  Bronze: land everything, change nothing

title: 6  Bronze: land everything, change nothing
text:
Faithful. Store what arrived, as text, with no cleaning. If the source says "12O", bronze says "12O".
Traceable. Every row carries _source_file, _source_system and _loaded_at.
Idempotent. Loading the same delivery twice must not create duplicates.
Additive. New deliveries are appended. Old ones are never edited, because they are your audit trail.
Tolerant. A new column in the source (schema drift) is recorded and flagged. It should not crash the pipeline.

title: 6  Bronze: land everything, change nothing
text:
6.2 Your first bronze table






🧠 Prompt 6.1 — bronze ingestion with lineage




Create a DuckDB warehouse with schemas bronze, silver, gold and ops. Write a function that loads a comma-separated values (CSV) into bronze. with every column as VARCHAR, and adds _source_file, _source_system and _loaded_at. Log each load (layer, table, row count) into ops.run_log. Load fmcg_sell_out.csv and show the lineage columns.



bronze_ingest() in R/kit.R is the reviewed answer:

bronze_ingest

function (con, file, table = NULL, system = "files", reader = NULL) 
{
    path <- raw_path(file)
    table <- table %||% gsub("[^a-z0-9]+", "_", tolower(tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(file))))
    ext <- tolower(tools::file_ext(file))
    reader <- reader %||% switch(ext, csv = sprintf("read_csv_auto(%s, all_varchar = true)", 
        sq(path)), parquet = sprintf("read_parquet(%s)", sq(path)), 
        json = sprintf("read_json_auto(%s)", sq(path)))
    dbExecute(con, sprintf("CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE bronze.%s AS\n     SELECT *, %s AS _source_file, %s AS _source_system, current_timestamp AS _loaded_at\n     FROM %s", 
        table, sq(basename(file)), sq(system), reader))
    n <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("SELECT COUNT(*) n FROM bronze.%s", 
        table))$n
    log_event(con, "bronze", table, n, basename(file))
    invisible(n)
}

title: 6  Bronze: land everything, change nothing
text:
6.3 Incremental, idempotent loading
Real sources arrive in instalments: a file every week, an extract every night. Reloading everything every time is wasteful, and appending blindly creates duplicates. The pattern is a load manifest: remember the fingerprint (Message-Digest Algorithm 5 (MD5) hash) of every file you have loaded, and skip the ones you’ve seen.






🧠 Prompt 6.2 — incremental loads with a manifest




Write ingest_increment(con, path, table) that (1) computes the file’s MD5, (2) skips it if ops.load_manifest already has that hash, (3) otherwise creates the bronze table on first load or appends with INSERT … BY NAME so new or re-ordered columns don’t break it, and (4) records the hash, file, rows and time in the manifest. Demonstrate with two deliveries of sell-out data, re-running the first to prove idempotency, and make the second delivery contain an extra column.




ingest_increment <- function(con, path, table) {
  dbExecute(con, "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ops.load_manifest (md5 VARCHAR, file VARCHAR, tbl VARCHAR, rows BIGINT, loaded_at TIMESTAMP)")
  md5 <- unname(tools::md5sum(path))
  if (nrow(dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT 1 FROM ops.load_manifest WHERE md5 = ?", params = list(md5)))) {
    message("SKIP (already loaded): ", basename(path)); return(invisible(0))
  }
  src <- sprintf("SELECT *, %s AS _source_file, current_timestamp AS _loaded_at
                  FROM read_csv_auto(%s, all_varchar = true)", sq(basename(path)), sq(path))
  if (!has_table(con, "bronze", table)) {
    dbExecute(con, sprintf("CREATE TABLE bronze.%s AS %s", table, src))
  } else {
    new_cols <- setdiff(names(dbGetQuery(con, paste(src, "LIMIT 0"))), names(dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("SELECT * FROM bronze.%s LIMIT 0", table))))
    for (c in new_cols) {                                      # schema drift: add the column, flag it
      dbExecute(con, sprintf('ALTER TABLE bronze.%s ADD COLUMN "%s" VARCHAR', table, c))
      message("SCHEMA DRIFT: new column '", c, "' in ", basename(path))
    }
    dbExecute(con, sprintf("INSERT INTO bronze.%s BY NAME %s", table, src))
  }
  n <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("SELECT COUNT(*) n FROM bronze.%s WHERE _source_file = %s", table, sq(basename(path))))$n

  invisible(n)
}

title: 6  Bronze: land everything, change nothing
text:
6.6 ✅ Mastery check

Why does bronze store every column as text?
What makes a load idempotent, and why does that matter at 3 a.m.?
What should happen when a source adds a column?








Solutions






So that bronze is faithful: it stores exactly what arrived, and no information is lost to type guessing. Bronze is the evidence. Silver does the typing, and it can always be rebuilt from bronze.
A load is idempotent when running it twice gives the same result as running it once. The load manifest does this: it records each file’s MD5 fingerprint and skips files already loaded. At 3 a.m., after a failure, anyone (or the scheduler) can simply re-run the pipeline without creating duplicates.
It should be tolerant: record and flag the new column (schema drift), add it to the bronze table (INSERT ... BY NAME), and leave older rows empty in it. It must not crash the run, and the column must not be silently dropped.

text:
6.7 🏢 In the organisation
Agree a delivery contract with every source owner, covering file name pattern, schedule, format, columns and who to call. Store bronze for at least as long as your audit and retention policy requires. The Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) requires that personal data is not kept longer than necessary, so bronze tables holding personal data need a documented retention period and a purge job (Chapter 15).

title: 7  Silver: clean, conform, remember
text:
7.2 Products and sell-out






🧠 Prompt 7.1 — the silver sell-out table




Write DuckDB SQL that builds silver.sell_out from bronze.fmcg_sell_out (all VARCHAR). Cast every column to its proper type. Treat blank units_sold and revenue_ngn as 0, because a blank means a stockout week (rule from the board pack Notes sheet), but keep a boolean units_was_blank as evidence. Keep exactly one row per (week_starting, depot_code, sku), preferring the earliest-loaded row. Comment every business rule.



This is the reviewed SQL, the same string the production script R/retail.R runs:

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE silver.sell_out AS 
SELECT CAST(week_starting AS DATE)                      AS week_starting,
       trim(depot_code)                                 AS depot_code,
       trim(sku)                                        AS sku,
       COALESCE(TRY_CAST(units_sold  AS DOUBLE), 0)     AS units_sold,
       TRY_CAST(unit_price_ngn AS DOUBLE)               AS unit_price_ngn,
       CAST(on_promotion  AS INTEGER)                   AS on_promotion,
       CAST(discount_pct  AS DOUBLE)                    AS discount_pct,
       CAST(stockout_flag AS INTEGER)                   AS stockout_flag,
       COALESCE(TRY_CAST(revenue_ngn AS DOUBLE), 0)     AS revenue_ngn,
       units_sold IS NULL                               AS units_was_blank   -- keep the evidence
FROM bronze.fmcg_sell_out
-- one row per business key: exact duplicates AND conflicting re-sends collapse to the first load
QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY week_starting, depot_code, sku ORDER BY rowid) = 1


CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE silver.products AS 
SELECT trim(sku)                         AS sku,
       trim(product_name)                AS product_name,
       trim(category)                    AS category,
       pack_size,
       CAST(unit_cost_ngn  AS DOUBLE)    AS unit_cost_ngn,
       CAST(list_price_ngn AS DOUBLE)    AS list_price_ngn
FROM bronze.fmcg_products
QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY trim(sku) ORDER BY rowid) = 1

Prove what changed between bronze and silver:

WITH c AS (
  SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM bronze.fmcg_sell_out)                  AS bronze_rows,
         (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM silver.sell_out)                       AS silver_rows,
         (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM silver.sell_out WHERE units_was_blank) AS stockout_blanks_kept_as_evidence)
SELECT bronze_rows, silver_rows, bronze_rows - silver_rows AS duplicates_removed, stockout_blanks_kept_as_evidence FROM c

“Which duplicate wins?” is a business decision



Of the duplicate keys, 211 are exact copies and 3 conflict (same key, different numbers). We keep the earliest-loaded row. The alternative, “latest wins”, is right when sources send corrections. The steward decides; the code records the decision. Write the rule in a comment, and test it (Chapter 9).

title: 7  Silver: clean, conform, remember
text:
7.3 Slowly Changing Dimensions: remembering history
The depot master lists DP04 twice: “Abuja Central”, and later “Abuja Central (Wuse II)”. The regional report’s footnote explains it: “Abuja Central includes Wuse II from Q3.” This is a slowly changing dimension: an attribute that changes rarely, but whose history matters.








Slowly changing dimension (SCD) type
Behaviour
Use when




Type 0
Never change
Original attributes (date opened)


Type 1
Overwrite: only the current value survives
Typos and corrections; history is not meaningful


Type 2
Add a new row with valid_from / valid_to / is_current
History matters: reorganisations, renames, price lists, an employee’s grade









🧠 Prompt 7.2 — SCD type 2




bronze.fmcg_depots lists DP04 twice (a rename). Build silver.depot_history as an SCD type 2 table: one row per depot version, ordered by load order, with valid_from (the opened date for version 1; 2025-10-01 for later versions, per a business confirmation), valid_to (the day before the next version starts) and is_current.




CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE silver.depot_history AS 
-- Slowly Changing Dimension type 2: keep every version of a depot.
-- Business rule (confirmed by Commercial): the DP04 rename took effect 2025-10-01.
WITH d AS (
  SELECT trim(depot_code) AS depot_code, trim(depot_name) AS depot_name,
         trim(region) AS region, trim(state) AS state, CAST(opened AS DATE) AS opened,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY trim(depot_code) ORDER BY rowid) AS version
  FROM bronze.fmcg_depots
), v AS (
  SELECT *, CASE WHEN version = 1 THEN opened ELSE DATE '2025-10-01' END AS valid_from FROM d
)
SELECT depot_code, version, depot_name, region, state, opened, valid_from,
       lead(valid_from) OVER (PARTITION BY depot_code ORDER BY version) - INTERVAL 1 DAY AS valid_to,
       lead(valid_from) OVER (PARTITION BY depot_code ORDER BY version) IS NULL         AS is_current
FROM v

text:
7.4 Tidy the presentation spreadsheet in SQL
The same Excel clean-up you did in R in Chapter 3, done in SQL inside the warehouse. The steps are: fill the merged cells, drop the total and footnote, unpivot the months, and parse the naira text.

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE silver.regional_report AS 
-- The printed Excel report, made tidy: fill merged region cells, unpivot months, parse '₦1,234'
WITH filled AS (
  SELECT last_value(region IGNORE NULLS) OVER (ORDER BY rowid) AS region, depot, * EXCLUDE (region, depot)
  FROM bronze.regional_report
  WHERE depot IS NOT NULL AND depot <> 'All depots'      -- drop the printed total and the footnote rows
), long AS (
  UNPIVOT filled ON Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep, Oct, Nov, Dec
  INTO NAME mon VALUE revenue_txt
)
SELECT region, depot AS depot_name,
       strptime('2025 ' || mon || ' 01', '%Y %b %d')::DATE                  AS month,
       CAST(regexp_replace(revenue_txt, '[^0-9.]', '', 'g') AS DOUBLE)       AS revenue_ngn
FROM long

7.6 Quarantine: rows you cannot fix
Some rows are simply wrong, like a 31-hour day. Don’t delete them and don’t let them through. Quarantine them: move them into a _rejects table with a reason, and let a test watch the reject count.

title: 7  Silver: clean, conform, remember
text:
7.8 ✅ Mastery check

Give two examples of a null that means something different from “unknown”.
When is SCD type 1 the right choice? When is type 2?
Why quarantine rather than delete?








Solutions






Examples: a blank units_sold that means a stockout week (zero sales, per the board pack’s Notes sheet), not a missing figure. A blank resolution date that means the complaint is still open. A blank “date left” that means the employee still works here. Each needs a documented rule and, ideally, an evidence flag such as units_was_blank.
Type 1 (overwrite) when history isn’t meaningful: typos and corrections. Type 2 (a new row with valid_from, valid_to, is_current) when history matters: renames and reorganisations, price lists, an employee’s grade.
Deleting destroys evidence and hides a problem in the source. Letting the row through corrupts the numbers. Quarantine keeps the row in a _rejects table with a reason, a test watches the reject count, and the source owner can fix it at source.

title: 7  Silver: clean, conform, remember
text:
7.9 🏢 In the organisation
Silver is where most of the organisation’s tacit knowledge becomes explicit. “We know Kaduna’s November data is off because of the re-segmentation” becomes a commented rule. Hold a monthly 30-minute data stewardship review: new anomalies, proposed rules, approvals. Minute it in the Git commit message.

title: 8  Gold: model for decisions
text:
8.1 Facts, dimensions and grain
🔵 Practitioner

title: 8  Gold: model for decisions
text:
A fact is a measurement of a business event: units sold, naira remitted, barrels produced, minutes of downtime. Facts are numbers you add up.
A dimension is the context you slice by: who, what, where, when. Depot, product, employer, well, week.
The grain is the exact meaning of one row in a fact table, stated in a sentence. Declare the grain before writing any Structured Query Language (SQL). Most modelling errors are grain errors.


Grain of gold.fct_sales: one row per week × depot × stock-keeping unit (SKU), recording units, revenue and gross profit for that combination.


8.1.1 Three kinds of fact table









Type
One row per…
Example
Typical question




Transaction
event
one purchase order (PO) line, one remittance, one complaint
“How many complaints came in via WhatsApp?”


Periodic snapshot
entity × period
depot × SKU × week; well × day; account × month-end
“What was the trend in weekly sales?”


Accumulating snapshot
process instance, updated as it progresses
a purchase order: ordered → shipped → received → paid
“Where do POs get stuck, and for how long?”

title: 8  Gold: model for decisions
text:
8.2 Build the star






🧠 Prompt 8.1 — a star schema from silver




From silver.sell_out, silver.products and silver.depot_history, build a star schema in gold: dim_product (with list margin), dim_depot (current version only), dim_week (year, quarter, year_month, International Organization for Standardization (ISO) week), and fct_sales at grain week × depot × SKU with gross_profit_ngn = revenue − units × unit cost. Then create a wide view gold.v_sales that pre-joins the star for business intelligence (BI) tools and the semantic layer, and a mart of revenue by depot and month.




CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold.dim_product AS 
SELECT sku, product_name, category, pack_size, unit_cost_ngn, list_price_ngn,
       round(1 - unit_cost_ngn / list_price_ngn, 3) AS list_margin
FROM silver.products


CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold.dim_depot AS 
SELECT depot_code, depot_name, region, state, opened
FROM silver.depot_history WHERE is_current


CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold.dim_week AS 
SELECT week_starting,
       year(week_starting)                      AS year,
       quarter(week_starting)                   AS quarter,
       strftime(week_starting, '%Y-%m')         AS year_month,
       weekofyear(week_starting)                AS iso_week
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT week_starting FROM silver.sell_out)


CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold.fct_sales AS 
-- Grain: one row per week x depot x SKU (a periodic snapshot fact)
SELECT s.week_starting, s.depot_code, s.sku,
       s.units_sold, s.revenue_ngn,
       s.revenue_ngn - s.units_sold * p.unit_cost_ngn AS gross_profit_ngn,
       s.on_promotion, s.discount_pct, s.stockout_flag
FROM silver.sell_out s
JOIN silver.products p USING (sku)


CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW gold.v_sales AS 
-- 'One big table' for the semantic layer and BI tools: the star, pre-joined
SELECT f.*, d.depot_name, d.region, d.state, p.product_name, p.category, p.pack_size,
       w.year, w.quarter, w.year_month
FROM gold.fct_sales f
JOIN gold.dim_depot   d USING (depot_code)
JOIN gold.dim_product p USING (sku)
JOIN gold.dim_week    w USING (week_starting)


CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold.mart_depot_month AS 
SELECT year_month, region, depot_code, depot_name,
       SUM(revenue_ngn) AS revenue_ngn, SUM(gross_profit_ngn) AS gross_profit_ngn,
       SUM(units_sold) AS units, AVG(stockout_flag) AS stockout_rate
FROM gold.v_sales GROUP BY ALL






The star: one fact in the centre, joined to each dimension by a single key.




Check the model with the question every star must answer cheaply: measure by dimension by dimension.

SELECT p.category, d.region, round(SUM(f.gross_profit_ngn) / SUM(f.revenue_ngn) * 100, 1) AS gross_margin_pct
FROM gold.fct_sales f
JOIN gold.dim_product p USING (sku)
JOIN gold.dim_depot   d USING (depot_code)
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 1, 2

title: 8  Gold: model for decisions
text:
8.4 An accumulating snapshot: purchase orders






🧠 Prompt 8.2 — accumulating snapshot




Using silver.purchase_orders (built in Chapter 7), build gold.fct_po_lifecycle with one row per PO: order date, received date, promised vs actual lead days, a delivery status (on time / late / date error), and the lateness in days. Then show on-time % and average lateness by conformed supplier.




if (!has_table(con, "silver", "purchase_orders")) {
  bronze_ingest(con, "supply_chain_pos.csv")
  run_sql(con, "silver", "purchase_orders", "SELECT po_id, CAST(po_date AS DATE) po_date, CAST(received_date AS DATE) received_date,
     CASE WHEN supplier_id = 'SUP-CEDAR-NG' THEN 'SUP-CEDAR' ELSE supplier_id END supplier_id, material_group,
     CAST(order_value_ngn AS DOUBLE) order_value_ngn, CAST(on_time AS INTEGER) on_time,
     CAST(received_date AS DATE) < CAST(po_date AS DATE) date_error FROM bronze.supply_chain_pos")
}
run_sql(con, "gold", "fct_po_lifecycle", "
  SELECT p.po_id, p.supplier_id, p.material_group, p.po_date, p.received_date, p.order_value_ngn,
         CAST(b.promised_lead_days AS INTEGER) AS promised_days,
         date_diff('day', p.po_date, p.received_date) AS actual_days,
         CASE WHEN p.date_error THEN 'date error'
              WHEN date_diff('day', p.po_date, p.received_date) <= CAST(b.promised_lead_days AS INTEGER) THEN 'on time'
              ELSE 'late' END AS delivery_status,
         greatest(date_diff('day', p.po_date, p.received_date) - CAST(b.promised_lead_days AS INTEGER), 0) AS days_late
  FROM silver.purchase_orders p JOIN bronze.supply_chain_pos b USING (po_id)")
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT supplier_id, COUNT(*) AS pos,
                        round(100 * AVG((delivery_status = 'on time')::INT), 1) AS on_time_pct,
                        round(AVG(days_late) FILTER (WHERE delivery_status = 'late'), 1) AS avg_days_late_when_late,
                        SUM((delivery_status = 'date error')::INT) AS date_errors
                 FROM gold.fct_po_lifecycle GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY on_time_pct")

8.5 🏋️ Exercises
E8.1 🟢 Write the grain sentence for gold.mart_depot_month. Is it a transaction, periodic snapshot or accumulating snapshot table?
E8.2 🟡 Build gold.fct_marketing_weekly (week × channel) with spend, conversions and cost per acquisition. Join it to weekly revenue to show spend vs revenue by week. What grain mismatch must you handle?
E8.3 🔴 Design (on paper, then in SQL) a gold model for pension remittances: dim_employer, dim_month, and fct_remittance at employer × month with expected, remitted, shortfall and days late. Add mart_compliance_month with compliance rate by sector.






Solutions





E8.1. “One row per calendar month × depot, with revenue, gross profit, units and stockout rate.” It is a periodic snapshot, aggregated from the weekly fact.

run_sql(con, "gold", "fct_marketing_weekly", "
  SELECT week_starting, channel, SUM(spend_ngn) spend_ngn, SUM(conversions) conversions,
         SUM(spend_ngn) / NULLIF(SUM(conversions), 0) AS cpa_ngn
  FROM silver.marketing_spend GROUP BY ALL")
dbGetQuery(con, "
  WITH m AS (SELECT week_starting, SUM(spend_ngn) spend FROM gold.fct_marketing_weekly GROUP BY 1),
       s AS (SELECT week_starting, SUM(revenue_ngn) revenue FROM gold.fct_sales GROUP BY 1)
  SELECT round(corr(spend, revenue), 3) AS weekly_correlation, COUNT(*) AS weeks
  FROM m JOIN s USING (week_starting)")

Correlation is not attribution, either. That needs an experiment (see the pensions playbook) or a marketing-mix model.

title: 8  Gold: model for decisions
text:
8.6 ✅ Mastery check

State the grain of three fact tables you know from your own organisation.
What makes a dimension “conformed”, and why does it matter?
When would you choose an accumulating snapshot?








Solutions






Model answers, one sentence each: one row per customer payment transaction; one row per employee per month-end, with headcount and pay; one row per purchase order, updated as it moves from ordered to received to paid. A good answer names the business event and every key that makes a row unique.
A dimension is conformed when every fact that uses it shares one version, with the same keys and the same attributes. Example: one dim_depot used by sales, inventory and deliveries. Then “revenue by region” and “deliveries by region” mean the same regions, and the facts can be compared side by side.
When you need to follow a process instance through its stages, such as a purchase order (ordered → shipped → received → paid), a loan application or a recruitment pipeline. You use it to answer “where do things get stuck, and for how long?”

title: 8  Gold: model for decisions
text:
8.7 🏢 In the organisation
Gold tables are products, and they need owners, documentation and change control. A change to fct_sales can break twenty dashboards, so treat it like an application programming interface (API) change: announce it, version it (v_sales_v2) and retire old versions on a schedule.

title: 9  Tests and the publish gate
text:
9.6 Designing good tests

Test the grain first. Uniqueness on the declared grain catches the most expensive errors.
Every business rule in silver gets a test in gold. “Blanks are stockouts” becomes “no null revenue”.
Reconcile to something outside the warehouse. Finance’s ledger, the regulator’s return, the bank statement. Internal consistency can’t prove accuracy.
Tune severity with the owner. A 0.5% reconciliation gap might be a warning in a weekly sales view and a hard failure in a regulatory return.
Keep tests fast. If the suite takes longer than the build, people will skip it.

9.7 🏋️ Exercises
E9.1 🟢 Add a test that gold.dim_depot has exactly 12 depots. Which kit function do you use?
E9.2 🟡 Write a test that compares the source’s on_time flag with the recomputed delivery_status in gold.fct_po_lifecycle, failing if they disagree on more than 2% of purchase orders (POs). Should it be error or warn?
E9.3 🔴 Write an anomaly test: fail if any depot’s revenue in the latest week is more than 3 standard deviations from its trailing 12-week mean. What are the risks of this kind of test?






Solutions






extra <- list(
  t_custom("dim_depot has 12 depots", "SELECT abs(COUNT(*) - 12) FROM gold.dim_depot"),
  t_custom("latest-week revenue within 3σ of trailing 12 weeks", "
    WITH w AS (SELECT depot_code, week_starting, SUM(revenue_ngn) r FROM gold.fct_sales GROUP BY ALL),
         s AS (SELECT *, AVG(r) OVER win mu, stddev(r) OVER win sd FROM w
               WINDOW win AS (PARTITION BY depot_code ORDER BY week_starting ROWS BETWEEN 12 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING))
    SELECT COUNT(*) FROM s WHERE week_starting = (SELECT MAX(week_starting) FROM w) AND abs(r - mu) > 3 * sd", sev = "warn"))
show_tests(run_tests(con, extra))

E9.1. Use t_custom(), because the expected count is a business fact rather than a generic rule. Alternatively, t_rowcount() with min 12, plus a uniqueness test.
E9.2. warn. A disagreement points to a data-entry or definition problem worth investigating, but it shouldn’t block the whole sales dashboard.
E9.3. Risks: (a) false alarms in seasonal weeks like Christmas and Ramadan, so compare with the same week last year; (b) small depots have high variance; (c) it is a warning signal, not proof of an error.

title: 9  Tests and the publish gate
text:
9.8 ✅ Mastery check

Name the eight test types and one failure each catches.
Why didn’t the reconciliation test catch the duplicated week?
What is the difference between error and warn severity in practice?








Solutions






unique: double loads, fan-out joins. not_null: broken extracts, failed casts. accepted_values: new, misspelt or unmapped codes. range: 31-hour days, negative stock, percentages stored on the wrong scale. relationships: orphan facts, missing master data. freshness: a stalled feed nobody noticed. volume: half a file, an empty delivery. reconciliation: everything else, including logic errors.
The duplicated week was in March 2026, while the reconciliation compares FY2025 revenue with the Excel report. The error was outside the period being reconciled, so the totals still agreed. The uniqueness test caught it. Each kind of test sees a different failure, which is why you need several.
error blocks publishing: the gate stays closed and yesterday’s version stays live. warn publishes but reports and alerts. Choose with the data owner. A 0.5% reconciliation gap might be a warning on a weekly sales view and an error on a regulatory return.
crumbs: 9  Tests and the publish gate

title: 9  Tests and the publish gate
text:
9.9 🏢 In the organisation
Tie the gate to a service level: “The sales dashboard refreshes by 07:00 with data to last Sunday. If tests fail, the Head of Commercial Finance is alerted by 06:30 and the previous version stays live.” That one sentence turns data quality from a technical worry into a managed commitment.

🟣 Advanced
A metric is more than a formula:

10.3 Metric trees: explaining why a number moved
Metrics are related. Revenue = units × average selling price, and gross profit = revenue × margin. A metric tree turns “revenue fell” into “volume held, price fell”, which is a different conversation entirely.






🧠 Prompt 10.2 — price-volume bridge




Using the semantic layer’s units and avg_selling_price metrics, decompose the change in revenue between Q4 2024 and Q4 2025 for each category into a volume effect and a price effect (with an interaction term), and show the bridge as a table.




pvm <- dbGetQuery(con, metric_sql(layer, c("revenue", "units", "avg_selling_price"), dims = "category",

                    sub(pattern = "SELECT ", replacement = "SELECT year, ") )
w <- reshape(pvm, idvar = "category", timevar = "year", direction = "wide")
with(w, data.frame(category,
  revenue_change_m = round((revenue.2025 - revenue.2024) / 1e6, 1),
  volume_effect_m  = round((units.2025 - units.2024) * avg_selling_price.2024 / 1e6, 1),
  price_effect_m   = round((avg_selling_price.2025 - avg_selling_price.2024) * units.2024 / 1e6, 1),

10.6 Governance of the layer itself

Version control. metrics.yml lives in Git, and every change is a reviewed pull request.
Ownership. One owner per metric. The owner approves changes.
Certification. Only certified metrics may appear in board packs and regulatory returns. exploratory ones carry a badge.
Change log. When a definition changes (for example, revenue becomes net of a new levy), note the effective date, and decide whether history is restated.

title: 10  The semantic layer: one definition of every KPI
text:
10.8 ✅ Mastery check

Why is the semantic layer the prerequisite for a trustworthy AI assistant?
Explain “sum first, divide last” to a non-analyst.
What is the difference between a certified and an exploratory metric?








Solutions






An AI assistant has to know what “revenue”, “active customer” or “margin” means in your organisation. Without one approved definition per metric, it invents its own, and each answer can differ from Finance’s. The semantic layer gives the model the certified definitions, so its SQL uses the same formulas as the board pack.
“If one shop sells ₦1,000 at 50% margin and another sells ₦1,000,000 at 10%, the business’s margin is not 30%. Add up all the profit, add up all the sales, then divide.” Totals first, then the ratio, so big and small units count by their size.
A certified metric has an owner, a version and an approval date, and it may appear in board packs and regulatory returns. An exploratory metric is useful for analysis but not yet approved. It carries a badge, and the compiler refuses it for board packs.

Start the semantic layer with the ten numbers the executive committee argues about. Put them in a two-hour workshop with their owners, agree the definitions in writing, and encode them the same week. Every later dashboard then inherits the agreement for free.

title: 11  Vector search and AI on governed data
text:
11.1 Embeddings in one picture
🟣 Advanced
An embedding turns a piece of text into a list of numbers, a point in space, so that texts with similar meaning land close together. Cosine similarity measures closeness: 1 means the same direction, 0 means unrelated. A vector index stores these points and finds the nearest neighbours of a query quickly.

Embedding method
How it works
Strengths
Weaknesses




Term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) (in kit.R)
Counts words, weights rare words up
Free, offline, explainable, instant
Matches words, not meaning; no synonyms; one language at a time


Neural sentence embeddings (e.g. all-MiniLM, multilingual-e5, OpenAI, Voyage)
A trained model maps meaning to ~384–3072 dimensions
Synonyms, paraphrase, cross-lingual (English ↔︎ Pidgin)
Needs a model or application programming interface (API); costs; data-protection review

The English query finds the English complaints about non-remittance and misses the Pidgin complaints describing exactly the same problem. The Pidgin query finds them, because it shares the words “oga”, “pension” and “enter”. TF-IDF matches words, so it cannot know that “oga dey remove pension but e no enter” means “my employer deducts but does not remit”. A regulator relying on it would under-count the problem among Pidgin speakers. That is a fairness issue, not just a technical one.
The fix is a multilingual neural embedding model, and the swap touches one function, embed():

hf_embed <- function(texts, model = "intfloat/multilingual-e5-small") {
  httr2::request(paste0("https://router.huggingface.co/hf-inference/models/", model, "/pipeline/feature-extraction")) |>
    httr2::req_auth_bearer_token(Sys.getenv("HF_TOKEN")) |>
    httr2::req_body_json(list(inputs = texts)) |> httr2::req_perform() |>
    httr2::resp_body_json(simplifyVector = TRUE)
}

11.4 Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
An large language model (LLM) knows nothing about your complaints. RAG fixes that in three steps:

Retrieve the most relevant records from the vector index.
Augment the prompt with them.
Let the model generate an answer that cites them.







🧠 Prompt 11.3 — a governed RAG prompt




Build a function that, for a question, retrieves the 8 most similar complaints and assembles a prompt instructing the model to answer only from those complaints, cite complaint identifiers (IDs), say “not enough evidence” if they don’t answer it, and never output personal data. Show the assembled prompt; call Claude only if ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set.




rag_prompt <- function(question, k = 8) {
  hits <- vector_search(con, idx, question, k = k)
  context <- paste(sprintf("[%s | %s | %s] %s", hits$complaint_id, hits$channel, hits$language, hits$complaint_text), collapse = "\n")
  paste0("You are a pensions customer-experience analyst.\n",
         "Answer ONLY from the complaints below. Cite complaint IDs in brackets. ",
         "If they do not answer the question, say 'not enough evidence'. Never reveal personal data.\n\n",
         "COMPLAINTS:\n", context, "\n\nQUESTION: ", question)
}
cat(rag_prompt("What are customers saying about updating their contact details?"))

You are a pensions customer-experience analyst.
Answer ONLY from the complaints below. Cite complaint IDs in brackets. If they do not answer the question, say 'not enough evidence'. Never reveal personal data.

COMPLAINTS:

[PC500001 | Web form | English] Online portal not showing my balance

ask_claude <- function(prompt, model = "claude-sonnet-5-5") {
  httr2::request("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages") |>
    httr2::req_headers(`x-api-key` = Sys.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"), `anthropic-version` = "2023-06-01") |>
    httr2::req_body_json(list(model = model, max_tokens = 600, messages = list(list(role = "user", content = prompt)))) |>
    httr2::req_perform() |> httr2::resp_body_json() |> (\(r) r$content[[1]]$text)()
}
cat(ask_claude(rag_prompt("What are customers saying about updating their contact details?")))

text:
11.5 Text-to-SQL, with guardrails
The Lab dashboard’s Ask your data page sends a question, plus the schema and the semantic-layer definitions (never the data rows), to a model that writes SQL. A human reviews the SQL, then it runs read-only. Each guardrail closes one specific risk:







Guardrail
Risk it closes




Semantic layer in the system prompt
The model inventing its own definition of “revenue”


Read-only connection + SELECT-only check
Prompt injection that tries to DROP TABLE


Row cap (LIMIT 5000)
Exfiltrating whole tables


SQL shown to the user before running
Silent wrong answers


Only schema + definitions sent, not rows
Personal data leaving the organisation (Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA))


Local model option (Ollama)
Any data leaving the laptop at all


Question → SQL → result logging
No audit trail


A golden-question test set
Quality drifting when the model or prompt changes









🧠 Prompt 11.4 — evaluate text-to-SQL




Build a small evaluation harness: a table of golden questions, each with a reference SQL. For each candidate SQL (from any model), run both, compare the results (same rows and values within 0.1%), and report accuracy. Include one deliberately wrong candidate to prove the harness catches it.




golden <- data.frame(
  question = c("How many complaints are still open?",
               "Which channel receives the most complaints?",
               "Average days to resolve complaints received in 2025"),
  reference = c("SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM silver.complaints WHERE status = 'open'",
                "SELECT channel FROM silver.complaints GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 1",
                "SELECT round(AVG(days_to_resolve),1) AS d FROM silver.complaints WHERE year(received_date) = 2025"),
  candidate = c("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM silver.complaints WHERE status = 'open'",
                "SELECT channel FROM silver.complaints GROUP BY channel ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 1",
                "SELECT round(AVG(days_to_resolve),1) FROM silver.complaints WHERE received_date >= DATE '2025-01-01'"))   # wrong: no upper bound, so 2026 is included
same <- function(a, b) isTRUE(all.equal(unname(as.list(a)), unname(as.list(b)), tolerance = 1e-3, check.attributes = FALSE))
golden$correct <- mapply(function(r, c) same(dbGetQuery(con, r), dbGetQuery(con, c)), golden$reference, golden$candidate)
golden[, c("question", "correct")]





question
correct




How many complaints are still open?
TRUE


Which channel receives the most complaints?
TRUE


Average days to resolve complaints received in 2025
FALSE





cat("Accuracy:", mean(golden$correct))

Accuracy: 0.6666667


The harness caught the subtle error. The candidate’s date filter has no upper bound, so it quietly includes 2026 complaints. This is exactly the kind of mistake that looks fine to a busy manager. Note also what the harness did not flag: both versions of the first question return the same count, even though one names its column n and the other doesn’t. The harness compares results, not wording.

text:
11.7 ✅ Mastery check

Explain an embedding and cosine similarity to a board member in three sentences.
Name four guardrails for text-to-SQL and the risk each removes.
Why is a golden-question test set necessary even if the model “seems good”?








Solutions






Model answer: “An embedding turns a piece of text into a list of numbers, a point on a map, so that texts with similar meanings sit close together. Cosine similarity measures how closely two points point the same way: 1 means the same meaning, 0 means unrelated. That lets us search complaints by what they mean, not by the exact words used.”
Any four of: semantic layer in the prompt, so the model doesn’t invent definitions; read-only connection and a SELECT-only check, against prompt injection such as DROP TABLE; row cap, against exfiltrating whole tables; SQL shown before it runs, against silent wrong answers; only schema and definitions sent, never rows, against personal data leaving the organisation; a local model option, so no data leaves the machine; logging question → SQL → result, for an audit trail.
Because “seems good” is an impression from a few questions, and it changes silently whenever the model, the prompt or the schema changes. A golden-question set (questions with reference SQL whose results are compared automatically) turns quality into a number you can re-check after every change.

title: 12  Serving: trusted data where people work
text:
12.9 ✅ Mastery check

Which target would you choose for a Power Apps field form, and why?
Why must serving targets be refreshed by the pipeline rather than by people?
What belongs in a serving contract?








Solutions






Microsoft Dataverse (or PostgreSQL, if the organisation isn’t Microsoft-first). Field forms need write-back and permissions. Dataverse is native to Power Apps, with security roles, and the form’s data becomes a source on the next pipeline run.
Hand-copying creates shadow versions: copies that skip the gate, go stale, and differ from each other. Refreshing from gold, after the gate and on a schedule, guarantees that every target shows the same tested numbers.
Stable names and columns (breaking changes get a new version and a retirement date), documented freshness (“refreshed daily by 07:00 with data to last Sunday”), an owner and a support route in the catalogue, and access defined by role, not by person.

13.2 Anatomy of a Quarto + Shiny dashboard
---
title: "TDBG Growth Cockpit"
format: dashboard          # (1) dashboard layout: pages, rows, columns, cards
server: shiny              # (2) a live R session powers the page
---

```{r}
#| context: setup          # (3) runs once per app: helpers, semantic layer, filter choices
source("R/helpers.R")
```

# {.sidebar}               # (4) a global sidebar: source picker + filters (inputs)
```{r}

dateRangeInput("dates", "Weeks", ...)
```

# Overview                 # (5) a page; "## Row" and "### Column" arrange cards
## Row {height=24%}
```{r}
uiOutput("kpis")           # (6) placeholders for outputs
```

```{r}
#| context: server         # (7) the reactive logic
warehouse_stamp <- reactivePoll(20000, session, checkFunc = function() file.mtime(db), valueFunc = ...)
sales  <- reactive({ warehouse_stamp(); get_sales(input$source, filters()) })   # re-runs when inputs or warehouse change
output$kpis <- renderUI({ semantic_frame(sales(), c("revenue", "gross_margin_pct")) |> value_boxes() })
```

title: 13  Dashboards with Quarto and Shiny
text:
13.3 How reactivity works
Shiny builds a dependency graph. Each output depends on the reactive values it reads. When an input or the warehouse file changes, only the outputs downstream of it recompute.





flowchart LR
  I1([input$source]) --> S[sales()]
  I2([input$dates]) --> F[filters() · debounced]
  I3([input$regions]) --> F
  F --> S
  W([warehouse file mtime<br/>reactivePoll]) --> S
  S --> K[KPI value boxes]
  S --> T[trend chart]
  S --> R[region chart]
  S --> P[top products table]
  W --> C[Connections page]






Performance rules that follow from the graph:

Filter in the database, not in R. get_sales() pushes the filters down as a SQL WHERE clause.
Debounce fast-changing inputs (debounce(400)), so dragging a date slider doesn’t fire twenty queries.
Compute each expensive thing once in a reactive() and share it. Never re-query inside each output.
Cache identical requests with bindCache(input$source, filters()).
Open short-lived, read-only connections, so the nightly rebuild can swap the warehouse file while users are on the page.

title: 13  Dashboards with Quarto and Shiny
text:
13.5 Design principles for decision dashboards

One page, one decision. Name the decision at the top: “Where should we restock this week?”
Read in a Z-pattern: KPIs (how are we doing?) → trend (which way?) → breakdown (where?) → detail (which ones?).
Every KPI has a comparison: target, last period or last year. A number alone is trivia.
Show definitions on hover, pulled from the semantic layer’s descriptions.
Show freshness and test status. “Data to 30 Mar 2026 · 12/12 tests passed” builds more trust than any colour scheme.
Accessible colour. Never rely on red and green alone; check contrast, and add labels.
Fast or forgotten. Interactions should respond in under one second.







🧠 Prompt 13.1 — design critique




Here is a screenshot of my dashboard [attach]. Critique it against these principles: one decision per page, Z-pattern reading order, comparisons on every KPI, definitions on hover, visible freshness and test status, accessible colour, and speed. Give the five highest-impact changes in priority order.

E13.1 🟢 Run the Lab dashboard (quarto serve 02-dashboard.qmd). Switch the source between comma-separated values (CSV), SQLite and DuckDB. What changes, and what doesn’t? Why?
E13.2 🟡 Add a “vs last year” delta to each KPI value box in the Lab dashboard, computed through the semantic layer.

Solutions





E13.1. The row counts and load times change. The KPIs don’t, because every source is cleaned by the same rules and measured through the same semantic layer. (Parquet is the exception to watch: it was cleaned elsewhere, earlier.)
E13.2 sketch. Compute sf(metrics) for the selected dates and for the same dates shifted by 52 weeks, then pass p(sprintf("%+.1f%% vs LY", 100*(cur/ly-1))) into value_box().
E13.3. The targets table is a source: the write-back loop in Figure 1.1. The next pipeline run lands it in bronze, validates it in silver (one target per region per quarter, numeric, positive), and joins it in gold. The dashboard reads targets from gold, never directly from the form’s table.

title: 13  Dashboards with Quarto and Shiny
text:
13.8 ✅ Mastery check

Static, Shiny or Shinylive? Pick one for a public teaching demo, a chief executive officer (CEO)’s daily cockpit, and a monthly emailed pack.
What does reactivePoll watch in the Lab dashboard, and why?
Name three performance rules and the problem each prevents.








Solutions






Public teaching demo: Shinylive (or a static dashboard), because it runs in the browser on any static host with no server. CEO’s daily cockpit: Shiny, because it is live, interactive and can be secured. Monthly emailed pack: static, rendered once to HTML by the scheduler and sent as a file.
It watches the modified time of the DuckDB warehouse file. When the nightly pipeline swaps in a new warehouse, every open dashboard notices and refreshes its data, without anyone reloading the page and without polling the database itself.
Any three of: filter in the database, so the app doesn’t pull whole tables into R; debounce fast inputs, so a dragged slider doesn’t fire twenty queries; compute once in a reactive(), so the same query doesn’t run for every chart; cache identical requests (bindCache), so repeat questions aren’t recomputed; short-lived read-only connections, so a lock doesn’t stop the nightly rebuild from swapping the file.

title: 14  Operations: run it every day without you
text:
14.1 The pipeline is a graph
⚫ Master
Every run is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of steps. A step runs only when its inputs are ready, and a failure stops everything downstream of it:
flowchart LR
  A[ingest: sell-out] --> D[silver: sell_out]
  B[ingest: products] --> E[silver: products]
  C[ingest: depots] --> F[silver: depot_history]
  X[ingest: regional report] --> Y[silver: regional_report]
  D & E --> G[gold: fct_sales]
  F --> H[gold: dim_depot]
  E --> I[gold: dim_product]
  G & H & I & Y --> T{tests}
  T -- pass --> P[publish: SQLite · Parquet · Postgres · Dataverse]
  T -- fail --> AL[alert + keep last good]
  P --> R[render reports & refresh dashboard]
crumbs: Level 4 · Master — Run it in production
14  Operations: run it every day without you

title: 14  Operations: run it every day without you
text:
14.2 A production-grade runner in 40 lines






🧠 Prompt 14.1 — a robust pipeline runner




Write run_platform() for my retail pipeline. It should: build into a temporary DuckDB file so the live warehouse is never half-built; time each step and log it; retry the ingest step up to 3 times with a back-off; run the tests; swap the new warehouse in only if the gate passes; otherwise keep the old file and raise an alert; and return a one-line status summary. Make it safe to run twice at the same time with a lock file.




run_platform <- function(live = "_platform/retail_live.duckdb", as_of = as.Date("2026-04-14"), alert = message) {
  lock <- paste0(live, ".lock")
  if (file.exists(lock)) stop("Another run is in progress (", lock, ")")
  file.create(lock); on.exit(unlink(lock), add = TRUE)
  tmp <- paste0(live, ".building"); unlink(c(tmp, paste0(tmp, ".wal")))
  con <- platform_connect(tmp); t0 <- Sys.time()
  step <- function(name, expr, retries = 0) {
    for (i in 0:retries) {
      s <- Sys.time()
      ok <- tryCatch({ force(expr); TRUE }, error = function(e) { alert(sprintf("[%s] attempt %d failed: %s", name, i + 1, conditionMessage(e))); FALSE })
      if (ok) { log_event(con, "step", name, round(as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), s, units = "secs")), 2), "seconds"); return(invisible(TRUE)) }
      Sys.sleep(2^i / 10)                                  # back-off before retrying
    }
    stop("Step failed after retries: ", name)
  }
  step("ingest", retail_bronze(con), retries = 2)
  step("silver", retail_run(con, "silver"))
  step("gold",   retail_run(con, "gold"))
  res <- run_tests(con, retail_tests(as_of = as_of))
  passed <- gate(res)
  dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
  if (passed) { unlink(live); file.rename(tmp, live) } else { alert("GATE CLOSED: live warehouse unchanged"); unlink(tmp) }
  sprintf("%s | %s | %d/%d tests passed | %.1fs", format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"),
          if (passed) "PUBLISHED" else "BLOCKED", sum(res$status == "PASS"), nrow(res),
          as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "secs")))
}
run_platform()

[1] "2026-10-15 17:18 | PUBLISHED | 12/12 tests passed | 1.4s"


Check the step timings from the log:

con <- dbConnect(duckdb(), "_platform/retail_live.duckdb", read_only = TRUE)
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT object AS step, rows AS seconds FROM ops.run_log WHERE layer = 'step'")





step
seconds




ingest
1


silver
0


gold
0





dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)







Five properties of a production pipeline




Atomic: consumers see the old version or the new one, never half of each (build to a temp file, then swap).
Idempotent: re-running after a failure is always safe (Chapter 6).
Observable: every step logs what it did and how long it took.
Guarded: tests decide whether to publish, and humans don’t (Chapter 9).
Exclusive: a lock stops two runs colliding.

text:
14.3 Scheduling








Where it runs
Scheduler
Good for




A laptop or office personal computer (PC)
macOS launchd, Linux cron, Windows Task Scheduler
Pilots. It breaks when the laptop sleeps


A small virtual machine (VM) or server
cron + Rscript refresh.R
Small teams; cheapest always-on option

14.5 The runbook






🧠 Prompt 14.2 — write the runbook




Write a one-page runbook for the nightly retail platform refresh: what it does, schedule and SLA, how to tell it failed, the five most likely failures with diagnosis and fix steps (source file late, schema drift, test failure, disk full, lock left behind), how to re-run safely, how to backfill a past week, and who to escalate to.



A runbook entry looks like this:

Failure: GATE CLOSED — unique(gold.fct_sales) failing. Likely cause: the source re-sent a week, or a delivery was double-dropped. Diagnose: SELECT _source_file, COUNT(*) FROM bronze.fmcg_sell_out GROUP BY 1 to see which file appeared twice. Fix: remove the duplicate delivery from the drop folder; re-run Rscript refresh.R. The manifest makes this safe. Escalate: if the source insists both files are valid, raise to the Commercial Finance steward. The rule “first load wins” may need to change.

teams_alert <- function(msg) {
  url <- Sys.getenv("TEAMS_WEBHOOK")
  if (!nzchar(url)) return(message("ALERT (no webhook set): ", msg))
  httr2::request(url) |> httr2::req_body_json(list(text = msg)) |> httr2::req_perform()
}

duration_watch <- function(log) {
  log |> dplyr::group_by(object) |>
    dplyr::summarise(median_s = median(rows), latest_s = dplyr::last(rows), .groups = "drop") |>
    dplyr::mutate(flag = latest_s > 2 * median_s)
}

title: 14  Operations: run it every day without you
text:
14.8 ✅ Mastery check

Name the five properties of a production pipeline.
Why does building into a temporary file and swapping matter to dashboard users?
How does keeping bronze make a backfill trivial?








Solutions






Atomic (users see the old version or the new one, never half of each), idempotent (re-running after a failure is safe), observable (every step logs what it did and how long it took), guarded (tests decide whether to publish, not people), exclusive (a lock stops two runs colliding).
The pipeline builds the new warehouse in a temporary file and renames it into place only after the gate passes. Users never see a half-built warehouse, and a failed run leaves the live file untouched.
Bronze keeps every delivery exactly as it arrived. When a silver or gold rule changes, or a bug is fixed, you rebuild silver and gold from bronze. There is no need to go back to the source systems for months of old extracts.

text:
15.2 Find personal data automatically






🧠 Prompt 15.1 — a personally identifiable information (PII) scanner




Write a function that scans every VARCHAR column of every table in a DuckDB schema and flags columns where more than 5% of a sample of values look like Nigerian phone numbers, email addresses, 11-digit identifiers (possible BVN or NIN), or personal names from a short list. Output a classification suggestion per column for the steward to confirm.




# A small table with personal data mixed in (synthetic)
dbWriteTable(con, DBI::Id(schema = "bronze", table = "contacts"), data.frame(
  customer_id = sprintf("C%05d", 1:6),
  full_name   = c("Ada Okafor", "Musa Bello", "Ngozi Eze", "Tunde Bakare", "Aisha Sani", "Emeka Obi"),
  phone       = c("08031234567", "+2348099876543", "07012345678", "09087654321", "08022223333", "08177778888"),
  email       = c("ada@example.ng", "musa@example.ng", NA, "tunde@example.ng", "aisha@example.ng", "emeka@example.ng"),
  bvn         = c("22212345678", "22298765432", "22233334444", "22255556666", "22277778888", "22299990000"),
  segment     = c("Mass", "Affluent", "Mass", "SME", "Mass", "Affluent")))
bronze_ingest(con, "bank_customers.csv")

scan_pii <- function(con, schema = "bronze", n = 500) {
  cols <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT table_name, column_name FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = ? AND data_type = 'VARCHAR'", params = list(schema))
  patterns <- c(phone = "^(\\+?234|0)[789][01]\\d{8}$", email = "^[^@ ]+@[^@ ]+\\.[a-z]{2,}$", id_11_digits = "^\\d{11}$",
                person_name = "^[A-Z][a-z]+ [A-Z][a-z]+$")
  out <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(cols)), function(i) {
    v <- na.omit(dbGetQuery(con, sprintf('SELECT "%s" v FROM %s.%s USING SAMPLE %d', cols$column_name[i], schema, cols$table_name[i], n))$v)
    hits <- vapply(patterns, function(p) mean(grepl(p, v)), 0)
    if (max(hits) > .05) data.frame(table = cols$table_name[i], column = cols$column_name[i],
                                    detected = names(which.max(hits)), share = round(max(hits), 2), suggested_class = "Restricted / personal")
  })
  do.call(rbind, out)
}
scan_pii(con)

15.3 Pseudonymise and mask

Pseudonymisation replaces an identifier with a consistent token. Analysts can still join and count, but can’t identify a person without the separately guarded key. (The pension employers file already does this: employer_name_hash.)
Masking shows partial values to roles that need to recognise, not read: 080******67.


salt <- Sys.getenv("PII_SALT", "demo-salt-store-me-in-a-vault")      # the secret that makes hashes irreversible in practice
run_sql(con, "silver", "contacts", sprintf("
  SELECT customer_id,
         sha256(%s || bvn)                                         AS bvn_token,      -- joinable, not reversible without the salt
         left(phone, 3) || '******' || right(phone, 2)             AS phone_masked,
         regexp_replace(email, '^(.).*@', '\\1***@')               AS email_masked,
         segment                                                   -- full_name dropped: not needed for analysis (minimisation)
  FROM bronze.contacts", sq(salt)))
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM silver.contacts LIMIT 3")

15.5 Secrets

Never in code, Git, Quarto documents or screenshots.
On laptops: .Renviron (git-ignored), or the operating system (OS) keychain via the keyring package.
On servers: the platform’s secret store (GitHub Actions secrets, Azure Key Vault, Posit Connect variables).

title: 15  Security, privacy and governance
text:
15.6 The NDPA 2023, in engineering terms







Principle (Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) 2023)
What it means for the platform




Lawful basis and purpose limitation
Record the purpose of each personal-data table in the catalogue; don’t reuse it for an unrelated purpose without a new basis


Data minimisation
Silver drops columns the purpose doesn’t need (we dropped full_name)


Accuracy
The tests and steward process are your accuracy controls


Storage limitation
Retention period per table, plus an automated purge job (below)


Integrity and confidentiality
Classification, roles, encryption at rest and in transit, secrets management


Accountability
DPIA for high-risk processing (AI on complaints, profiling); audit logs; a named DPO


Data subject rights
Be able to find a person’s data (lineage + pseudonym keys) to answer access and erasure requests


Breach notification
Detect (logs, alerts) and know whom to notify, and how fast, under the Act and the NDPC’s directives


Cross-border transfer
Know where your cloud region and AI provider process data



The General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID) 2025 (the NDPC’s General Application and Implementation Directive) adds implementation detail, including DPIA and audit expectations. Sector regulators add more: CBN for banks, PenCom for pension operators, NCC for telecoms.
