title: 15  Security, privacy and governance
text:
15.9 ✅ Mastery check

What is the difference between pseudonymisation and masking? When do you use each?
Name five NDPA principles and the platform control that implements each.
Which data may go to an external AI API in your organisation today, and who decided?








Solutions






Pseudonymisation replaces an identifier with a consistent token (e.g. employer_name_hash). Analysts can still join and count, but can’t identify the person without the separately guarded key. Use it in analytical tables. Masking shows a partial value (080******67) to people who need to recognise a record, not read it, such as a support agent confirming a caller.
Any five: lawful basis and purpose limitation, recorded per table in the catalogue; data minimisation, silver drops unneeded columns; accuracy, the tests and the steward process; storage limitation, a retention period and an automated purge job; integrity and confidentiality, classification, roles, encryption and secrets management; accountability, DPIAs, audit logs, a named DPO; data subject rights, lineage and pseudonym keys to find a person’s data; breach notification, logs and alerts; cross-border transfer, knowing where cloud and AI providers process data.
A personal answer, but a complete one names: the classes of data allowed (e.g. public and internal, and schema-only for confidential tables); what is excluded (restricted and personal data, unless there is a lawful basis, an agreement with the provider and a DPIA); and who decided: the DPO, with the data owner, recorded in a policy. “Nobody has decided” is the most common answer, and the one to fix first.

Licences bought, nothing used
Prove value on DuckDB first; buy when a graduation trigger fires


Governance theatre
Policies nobody follows
Controls as code: tests, roles, purge jobs


AI before data
A confident chatbot with wrong answers
Gate + semantic layer + golden-question tests first

title: 16  Deploying in an organisation
text:
16.10 ✅ Mastery check

Why must production never be edited by hand?
Which operating model fits your organisation today, and what would trigger moving to the next?
What is the first use case you would choose, and why that one?








Solutions






Because a hand edit has no record, no review and no test. It can’t be reproduced, and the next pipeline run silently overwrites it. Every change goes through Git, review and CI, so production is always the result of versioned code.
Usually centralised for the first 12–18 months: one team builds the platform and the first use cases. Move to hub-and-spoke when business units queue for the central team and have analysts who can build their own marts on shared gold. Move to federated only when domain teams are strong enough to own data products end to end.
Pick for pain, not glamour. Choose the report that costs the most people the most time every month, with a clear owner and data you can get. Example: the monthly sales pack that takes three analysts a week. Success is visible, and it builds the bronze, silver and gold the next use cases reuse.

title: 16  Deploying in an organisation
text:
16.11 🏢 In the organisation
The architecture is easy to copy; the operating model is not. Organisations that succeed treat data as a product, with owners, users, a service level and a roadmap, rather than as a by-product of IT systems.

title: 17  Playbook: Human resources
text:
17.1 Decisions this platform supports
Sector People analytics: attrition, pay equity, engagement

title: 17  Playbook: Human resources
text:
Retention: who is likely to leave in the next 12 months, and what can a manager do about it?
Pay: is pay consistent within grades? Are there unexplained gaps?
Workforce planning: headcount, span of control and promotion velocity by department.
Engagement: where is engagement falling, and does it predict exits?

title: 17  Playbook: Human resources
text:
17.2 Architecture mapped to HR







Layer
In human resources (HR)




Sources
Human resources information system (HRIS) (SAP SuccessFactors, Workday, Dynamics 365 HR in Dataverse, Oracle human capital management (HCM), or Excel), payroll, the engagement survey tool, the learning system, recruitment applicant tracking system (ATS), exit interviews (text)


Bronze
Monthly HRIS extract + payroll file + survey export, as delivered


Silver
Typed employees; one row per employee per snapshot; grades conformed across business units; outcome-leaking fields removed from analytical tables


Gold
fct_employee_month (periodic snapshot), dim_department, dim_grade; mart_attrition_risk


Gate
Unique employee per snapshot; valid grades; engagement within 1–5; pay > 0; headcount reconciles to payroll


Govern
Metrics: headcount, attrition rate, regretted attrition, compa-ratio, engagement index. Vector index over exit-interview text


Serve
Human resources business partner (HRBP) dashboard (Shiny, with row-level security by department); Dataverse for HR Power Apps; aggregate-only views for executives


Plane
Pay and performance are confidential; names and identifiers (IDs) are personal. Data protection impact assessment (DPIA) for any predictive model about people

title: 17  Playbook: Human resources
text:
17.3 Run the pipeline






🧠 Prompt 17.1 — HR pipeline




Build an HR pipeline with the kit’s run_pipeline(): bronze from hr_attrition.csv; silver.employees typed, with exit_interview_booked excluded because it leaks the outcome; gold.fct_employee with a compa-ratio (pay ÷ median pay for the grade), an engagement band and a promotion-wait band; and a department mart. Tests: unique employee_id, engagement 1–5, pay > 0, accepted grades and work patterns. Publish the mart to a serving SQLite file.




spec <- list(
  name = "hr",
  bronze = list(hr_attrition = "hr_attrition.csv"),
  silver = list(employees = "
    SELECT employee_id, department, grade, CAST(annual_pay_ngn AS DOUBLE) AS annual_pay_ngn,
           CAST(tenure_years AS DOUBLE) AS tenure_years, CAST(commute_minutes AS DOUBLE) AS commute_minutes,
           CAST(engagement_score AS DOUBLE) AS engagement_score, CAST(months_since_promotion AS DOUBLE) AS months_since_promotion,
           CAST(training_hours_12m AS DOUBLE) AS training_hours_12m, CAST(manager_span AS INTEGER) AS manager_span,
           work_pattern, CAST(left_within_12m AS INTEGER) AS left_within_12m
           -- exit_interview_booked deliberately excluded: it is recorded after resignation (target leakage)
    FROM bronze.hr_attrition"),
  gold = list(
    fct_employee = "
      SELECT *, annual_pay_ngn / median(annual_pay_ngn) OVER (PARTITION BY grade) AS compa_ratio,
             CASE WHEN engagement_score < 3 THEN 'low' WHEN engagement_score < 4 THEN 'mid' ELSE 'high' END AS engagement_band,
             CASE WHEN months_since_promotion >= 6 THEN '6+ months' WHEN months_since_promotion >= 3 THEN '3-6 months' ELSE '< 3 months' END AS promo_wait_band
      FROM silver.employees",
    mart_department = "
      SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount, AVG(left_within_12m) AS attrition_rate,
             AVG(engagement_score) AS engagement, median(annual_pay_ngn) AS median_pay, AVG(manager_span) AS avg_span
      FROM gold.fct_employee GROUP BY 1"),
  tests = list(
    t_unique("gold.fct_employee", "employee_id"),
    t_range("gold.fct_employee", "engagement_score", 1, 5),
    t_range("gold.fct_employee", "annual_pay_ngn", 1),
    t_accepted("gold.fct_employee", "work_pattern", c("Onsite", "Hybrid", "Remote")),
    t_accepted("gold.fct_employee", "grade", c("Analyst", "Senior Analyst", "Manager", "Senior Manager", "Director")),
    t_rowcount("gold.fct_employee", 1000)),
  publish = c("gold.mart_department"))
hr <- run_pipeline(spec)
show_tests(hr$tests); cat("Published:", hr$published)

text:
17.4 Insight: what drives attrition?

d <- dbGetQuery(hr$con, "SELECT engagement_band, promo_wait_band, AVG(left_within_12m) attrition, COUNT(*) n
                         FROM gold.fct_employee GROUP BY ALL")
d$engagement_band <- factor(d$engagement_band, c("low", "mid", "high"))
d$promo_wait_band <- factor(d$promo_wait_band, c("< 3 months", "3-6 months", "6+ months"))
ggplot(d, aes(promo_wait_band, engagement_band, fill = attrition)) + geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(attrition, 1)), colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#7FA8D4", high = "#0B2C55", labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Time since last promotion", y = "Engagement", fill = "12-month attrition",
       title = "Attrition by engagement and promotion wait")









17.4.1 The leakage lesson, in numbers






🧠 Prompt 17.2 — prove the leakage




Fit two logistic regressions for left_within_12m: one with exit_interview_booked (from bronze), one without (from gold). Compare their area under the curve (AUC) on a 30% hold-out. Explain to an HR director why the “better” model is useless.




auc <- function(y, p) { r <- rank(p); n1 <- sum(y); (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * (length(y) - n1)) }
full <- dbGetQuery(hr$con, "SELECT g.*, CAST(b.exit_interview_booked AS INTEGER) AS exit_interview_booked
                            FROM gold.fct_employee g JOIN bronze.hr_attrition b USING (employee_id)")
set.seed(7); test <- sample(nrow(full), .3 * nrow(full))
f_honest <- left_within_12m ~ engagement_score + months_since_promotion + compa_ratio + tenure_years + commute_minutes + training_hours_12m + work_pattern
f_leaky  <- update(f_honest, . ~ . + exit_interview_booked)
m1 <- glm(f_honest, binomial, full[-test, ]); m2 <- suppressWarnings(glm(f_leaky, binomial, full[-test, ]))
data.frame(model = c("honest (no leakage)", "with exit_interview_booked"),
           hold_out_AUC = round(c(auc(full$left_within_12m[test], predict(m1, full[test, ])),
                                  auc(full$left_within_12m[test], predict(m2, full[test, ]))), 3))

The leaky model scores almost perfectly, because it is told who has already resigned. The honest model is the one that can warn a manager before the resignation. Its top drivers (engagement, promotion wait, pay position) are things a manager can act on.

title: 17  Playbook: Human resources
text:
17.6 Deploying in an HR function

Owner: the chief human resources officer (CHRO) owns the definitions; the HR analytics lead owns the pipeline.
First 90 days: a monthly attrition and headcount pack that reconciles to payroll; then a flight-risk list for HRBPs, with reasons, not just scores.
Privacy: individual risk scores are personal data about employees. You need a DPIA, a clear lawful basis, access limited to the employee’s own HRBP and manager, and no automated decisions. The model prompts a conversation, never a dismissal.
Fairness: do not use protected characteristics as model inputs. Check outcomes across groups where lawful.
Pitfall: the HRIS records reasons for leaving after the fact. Keep them for reporting, never as model features.

title: 17  Playbook: Human resources
text:
17.7 🏋️ Exercises
E17.1 🟢 Which department has the highest attrition, and what is its median pay relative to the company? E17.2 🟡 Add a test that fails if any grade’s compa-ratio spread (max ÷ min) exceeds 3. Investigate any failure: data error or pay-equity issue? E17.3 🔴 Build a “manager pack”: for each department, the five employees with the highest honest-model risk, their top driver, and a suggested action. What access controls must this output have?

title: 17  Playbook: Human resources
text:
17.8 ✅ Mastery check

Why must exit_interview_booked be kept out of the analytical tables, and how would you prove the harm to an HR director?
What is a compa-ratio, and what might a very wide spread within one grade mean?
What safeguards must a flight-risk list have before human resources business partners see it?








Solutions






An exit interview is booked only after someone resigns, so the field leaks the outcome. Prove it with two models scored on the same hold-out: the leaky one reaches an AUC of about 0.97, the honest one about 0.73. The “better” model only recognises people who have already left; it can never warn a manager in time.
Pay ÷ the median pay for the grade. 1.0 means paid at the grade median. A very wide spread (e.g. max ÷ min above 3) is either a data error (a wrong grade, monthly vs annual pay) or a pay-equity issue. The test flags it, and a person investigates which.
A DPIA and a lawful basis; access limited to the employee’s own HRBP and manager (row-level security by department); reasons, not just scores; no automated decisions, because the list prompts a conversation, never a dismissal; and no protected characteristics as model inputs.

title: 18  Playbook: Education
text:
18.1 Decisions this platform supports
Sector Schools, universities and training providers: progression, attendance, early warning

title: 18  Playbook: Education
text:
Early warning: which learners are at risk of failing or dropping out this term, early enough to help?
Teaching quality: which courses have unusual pass rates or score distributions?
Capacity: enrolment trends by programme and campus.
Accreditation and returns: consistent numbers for the regulator (National Universities Commission (NUC), National Board for Technical Education (NBTE), state ministries) and for accreditation bodies.

title: 18  Playbook: Education
text:
18.2 Architecture mapped to education







Layer
In education




Sources
Student information system, learning management system (Moodle, Canvas, Google Classroom), attendance registers (often paper or Excel), the exam and grading system, fees and finance, surveys


Silver
One learner per real person (matric numbers conformed: case, spaces, old and new formats); scores validated 0–100; attendance ≤ sessions held


Gold
fct_assessment (learner × course × assessment), fct_attendance_week, dim_learner, dim_course, mart_early_warning


Gate
Unique learner identifiers (IDs); score ranges; attendance ≤ sessions; every enrolment points at a real course; term totals reconcile to the registry


Govern
Metrics: pass rate, mean score, attendance rate, at-risk count. Definitions agreed with the academic board


Serve
Course-leader dashboards; adviser lists; registry SQLite mart; Portable Document Format (PDF) returns to the regulator


Plane
Learners may be minors. Their data needs extra care: strict roles, minimal fields, guardians’ rights, and no external artificial intelligence (AI) on identifiable records

title: 18  Playbook: Education
text:
18.3 Data (synthetic, generated reproducibly)
There is no education dataset in the course folder, so we generate a realistic one, with planted problems.

set.seed(2026)
n <- 1200
learners <- data.frame(matric = sprintf("LBS/%04d", 1:n),
                       programme = sample(c("BSc Economics", "BSc Accounting", "BSc Data Science", "BSc Business Admin"), n, TRUE),
                       entry_year = sample(2023:2025, n, TRUE), campus = sample(c("Lekki", "Ikeja", "Abuja"), n, TRUE, prob = c(.5, .3, .2)))
learners$matric[c(15, 400)] <- c("lbs/0015 ", "LBS/0400 ")        # planted: same learner, inconsistent IDs
learners <- rbind(learners, transform(learners[c(15, 400), ], matric = c("LBS/0015", "LBS/0400")))
courses <- data.frame(course = c("ECO101", "ACC102", "DSC103", "BUS104", "STA105", "MKT106"),
                      sessions_per_week = c(3, 3, 4, 2, 3, 2))
grid <- merge(data.frame(matric = sprintf("LBS/%04d", 1:n), ability = rnorm(n)), courses)
grid <- grid[runif(nrow(grid)) < .6, ]                                      # each learner takes ~60% of courses
grid$attended <- pmin(rbinom(nrow(grid), 12 * grid$sessions_per_week, plogis(1.6 + .8 * grid$ability)), 12 * grid$sessions_per_week)
grid$score <- round(pmin(100, pmax(0, 55 + 12 * grid$ability + 25 * (grid$attended / (12 * grid$sessions_per_week) - .75) + rnorm(nrow(grid), 0, 9))))
grid$score[sample(nrow(grid), 6)] <- c(105, 110, 101, 120, 104, 999)          # planted: impossible scores
grid$attended[sample(nrow(grid), 4)] <- 60                                     # planted: attended > sessions
enrolments <- grid[, c("matric", "course", "attended", "score")]
c(learners = nrow(learners), enrolments = nrow(enrolments))

  learners enrolments 
      1202       4293

title: 18  Playbook: Education
text:
18.4 Run the pipeline

spec <- list(
  name = "education",
  bronze = list(learners = learners, courses = courses, enrolments = enrolments),
  silver = list(
    learners = "SELECT DISTINCT upper(trim(matric)) AS matric, programme, CAST(entry_year AS INTEGER) entry_year, campus FROM bronze.learners",
    enrolments = "
      SELECT upper(trim(e.matric)) AS matric, e.course, CAST(e.attended AS INTEGER) attended,
             12 * c.sessions_per_week AS sessions_held, CAST(e.score AS DOUBLE) score
      FROM bronze.enrolments e JOIN bronze.courses c USING (course)
      WHERE CAST(e.score AS DOUBLE) BETWEEN 0 AND 100 AND CAST(e.attended AS INTEGER) <= 12 * c.sessions_per_week",
    enrolment_rejects = "
      SELECT e.*, 'score outside 0-100 or attendance > sessions' AS reason
      FROM bronze.enrolments e JOIN bronze.courses c USING (course)
      WHERE NOT (CAST(e.score AS DOUBLE) BETWEEN 0 AND 100 AND CAST(e.attended AS INTEGER) <= 12 * c.sessions_per_week)"),
  gold = list(
    fct_enrolment = "SELECT *, attended / sessions_held AS attendance_rate, (score >= 50)::INT AS passed FROM silver.enrolments",
    mart_early_warning = "
      SELECT e.matric, l.programme, l.campus, COUNT(*) AS courses, AVG(e.attendance_rate) AS attendance_rate,
             AVG(e.score) AS mean_score, SUM(1 - e.passed) AS courses_failing,
             (AVG(e.attendance_rate) < 0.75 AND AVG(e.score) < 50) AS at_risk
      FROM gold.fct_enrolment e JOIN silver.learners l USING (matric) GROUP BY ALL"),
  tests = list(
    t_unique("silver.learners", "matric"),
    t_unique("gold.fct_enrolment", c("matric", "course")),
    t_range("gold.fct_enrolment", "score", 0, 100),
    t_range("gold.fct_enrolment", "attendance_rate", 0, 1),
    t_relationship("gold.fct_enrolment", "matric", "silver.learners"),
    t_custom("rejected enrolments ≤ 0.5% (else stop and ask the registry)",
             "SELECT CASE WHEN (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM silver.enrolment_rejects) > 0.005 * (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM bronze.enrolments) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END")),
  publish = c("gold.mart_early_warning"))
ed <- run_pipeline(spec)

title: 18  Playbook: Education
text:
18.6 Deploying in an institution

Owner: the registrar (data) and the academic board (definitions such as “at risk”).
First 90 days: a weekly attendance feed from the learning management system (LMS) and registers, then an adviser list every Monday.
Ethics: “at risk” labels can stigmatise. Use them for support, never for sanctions. Explain the criteria to learners.
Minors: where learners are under 18, apply stricter access and retention, and involve the data protection officer (DPO) before any analytics beyond statutory reporting.

title: 18  Playbook: Education
text:
18.7 🏋️ Exercises
E18.1 🟢 Which campus has the highest share of at-risk learners? E18.2 🟡 Add a course-level mart with pass rate, mean score and score standard deviation. Flag courses whose pass rate is more than 2 standard deviations from the mean of all courses. E18.3 🔴 Make the early-warning rule weekly: simulate 12 weeks of attendance, and find the earliest week at which the rule identifies 80% of eventual failures.

title: 18  Playbook: Education
text:
18.8 ✅ Mastery check

Why is attendance a better early-warning signal than exam scores?
What does “conforming” learner IDs mean, and what problem did it fix in this playbook?
What extra controls apply when some learners are under 18?








Solutions






Attendance is known weeks before exam results. An adviser can call a learner in week 4 and still change the outcome; an exam score only says what has already happened.
Bringing every spelling of the same ID to one standard form (here upper(trim()), and mapping old and new matric formats) so each real learner has one ID. It merged learners who had been recorded twice, which would otherwise have been counted as two people.
Stricter roles and retention, minimal fields, respect for guardians’ rights, no external AI on identifiable records, and the DPO involved before any analytics beyond statutory reporting. “At risk” labels are used for support, never for sanctions, and the criteria are explained to learners.

title: 19  Playbook: Supply chain and procurement
text:
19.1 Decisions this platform supports
Sector Supplier performance, lead times, inventory risk
crumbs: 19  Playbook: Supply chain and procurement

title: 19  Playbook: Supply chain and procurement
text:
Supplier management: who delivers on time and in full, and who should get more or less business?
Inventory policy: how much safety stock do we need, given actual lead-time variability?
Import logistics: which port and incoterm combinations are slow or unpredictable?
Stockout prevention: linking late inbound deliveries to outbound stockouts (with the retail sell-out data).
crumbs: 19  Playbook: Supply chain and procurement

title: 19  Playbook: Supply chain and procurement
text:
19.2 Architecture mapped to supply chain







Layer
In supply chain




Sources
Enterprise resource planning (ERP) purchasing (SAP MM, Dynamics 365 supply chain management (SCM), Oracle), warehouse management system (WMS) goods receipts, freight forwarders’ files, port and customs data, supplier portals, Excel trackers


Silver
Typed purchase orders (POs); conformed supplier master (SUP-CEDAR = SUP-CEDAR-NG); date errors flagged (received before ordered); one row per PO line


Gold
fct_po_lifecycle (accumulating snapshot: ordered → received); dim_supplier; mart_supplier_scorecard; mart_lead_time_stats


Gate
Unique PO; received ≥ ordered (or quarantined); order value = qty × unit cost; every supplier in the master; spend reconciles to accounts payable


Govern
Metrics: on time in full (OTIF) %, mean and standard deviation of lead time, spend, supplier concentration (top-3 share)


Serve
Procurement dashboard; supplier scorecards (Portable Document Format (PDF)) for quarterly reviews; safety-stock parameters back to the ERP


Plane
Supplier prices are confidential; contract data is restricted to procurement
crumbs: 19  Playbook: Supply chain and procurement

title: 19  Playbook: Supply chain and procurement
text:
19.3 Run the pipeline

spec <- list(
  name = "supply_chain",
  bronze = list(pos = "supply_chain_pos.csv",
                map_supplier = data.frame(source_code = "SUP-CEDAR-NG", conformed_code = "SUP-CEDAR",
                                          reason = "Nigerian subsidiary; same contract")),
  silver = list(
    purchase_orders = "
      SELECT p.po_id, CAST(p.po_date AS DATE) po_date, CAST(p.received_date AS DATE) received_date,
             COALESCE(m.conformed_code, p.supplier_id) AS supplier_id, p.supplier_id AS supplier_id_source,
             p.material_group, p.incoterm, p.port_of_entry,
             CAST(p.order_qty AS INTEGER) order_qty, CAST(p.unit_cost_ngn AS DOUBLE) unit_cost_ngn,
             CAST(p.order_value_ngn AS DOUBLE) order_value_ngn, CAST(p.promised_lead_days AS INTEGER) promised_days
      FROM bronze.pos p LEFT JOIN bronze.map_supplier m ON p.supplier_id = m.source_code
      WHERE CAST(p.received_date AS DATE) >= CAST(p.po_date AS DATE)",
    po_rejects = "SELECT *, 'received before ordered' AS reason FROM bronze.pos WHERE CAST(received_date AS DATE) < CAST(po_date AS DATE)"),
  gold = list(
    fct_po_lifecycle = "
      SELECT *, date_diff('day', po_date, received_date) AS actual_days,
             (date_diff('day', po_date, received_date) <= promised_days)::INT AS on_time
      FROM silver.purchase_orders",
    mart_supplier_scorecard = "

19.5 Insight 2: safety stock from real variability
Safety stock protects against variability, not averages. A standard formula, for demand d per day with standard deviation σ_d, and lead time L with standard deviation σ_L:
\[SS = z \sqrt{\bar{L}\,\sigma_d^2 + \bar{d}^2 \sigma_L^2}\]

z <- qnorm(0.95)              # 95% cycle service level
d_bar <- 400; sd_d <- 120     # illustrative daily demand for one material
s |> transform(safety_stock_units = round(z * sqrt(mean_lead * sd_d^2 + d_bar^2 * sd_lead^2))) |>
  subset(select = c(supplier_id, mean_lead, sd_lead, safety_stock_units)) |> head(9)

19.7 Deploying in a supply-chain function

Owner: Head of Procurement (supplier master and scorecard definitions); Supply Planning (safety-stock parameters).

title: 19  Playbook: Supply chain and procurement
text:
19.9 ✅ Mastery check

What does OTIF measure, and why must the supplier master be conformed before you calculate it?
Why does safety stock depend on lead-time variability rather than the average lead time?
Why report the 90th-percentile lead time next to the mean?








Solutions






On time in full: the share of orders delivered by the promised date and in the full quantity. If SUP-CEDAR and SUP-CEDAR-NG stay separate, one supplier’s record is split in two, its scorecard is wrong, and spend concentration is understated.
Safety stock protects against surprises. Using \(SS = z\sqrt{\bar{L}\sigma_d^2 + \bar{d}^2\sigma_L^2}\), two suppliers with the same average lead time but different spread need very different buffers. Moving a material to a predictable supplier releases working capital, which is the business case for the scorecard.
Planners are hurt by the slow tail, not the average. The 90th percentile says “one shipment in ten takes longer than this”, which is what a buffer and a promise to customers must cover.

20.1 Architecture mapped to retail
Sector Store and depot performance, promotions, baskets, experiments
The running example (Chapters 6–13) is a retail and fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) platform. This playbook adds the three analyses retail leaders ask for next: promotion effectiveness, basket economics and trustworthy A/B tests.

20.2 Promotion effectiveness






🧠 Prompt 20.1 — promo uplift




Using gold.v_sales, estimate promotion uplift: for each category, compare average units per depot-SKU-week on promotion vs off promotion, within the same depot and SKU, so that big depots don’t bias the result. Then compute the incremental gross profit after discount. Which categories’ promotions pay for themselves?




con <- platform_connect("_platform/retail.duckdb")
if (!has_table(con, "gold", "fct_sales")) retail_build(con)
dbExecute(con, paste("CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW gold.v_sales AS", retail_sql[["gold.v_sales"]]))

promo <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  WITH cell AS (   -- same depot and SKU, promo vs non-promo weeks
    SELECT category, depot_code, sku,
           AVG(units_sold)       FILTER (WHERE on_promotion = 1) AS units_promo,
           AVG(units_sold)       FILTER (WHERE on_promotion = 0) AS units_base,
           AVG(gross_profit_ngn) FILTER (WHERE on_promotion = 1) AS gp_promo,
           AVG(gross_profit_ngn) FILTER (WHERE on_promotion = 0) AS gp_base
    FROM gold.v_sales WHERE stockout_flag = 0 GROUP BY ALL)
  SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS depot_sku_cells,
         round(100 * (AVG(units_promo / units_base) - 1), 1) AS volume_uplift_pct,
         round(100 * (AVG(gp_promo / gp_base) - 1), 1)       AS gross_profit_uplift_pct

20.4 Experiments you can trust






🧠 Prompt 20.2 — read an A/B test properly




Analyse ab_test_checkout.csv (arm, device, converted, revenue_ngn). First check for sample-ratio mismatch (SRM) against the intended 50/50 split, overall and by device, with a chi-square test. Only then compare conversion and revenue per user between arms with confidence intervals. Explain why SRM invalidates the naive result.

run_sql(con, "gold", "fct_experiment_user", "SELECT user_id, arm, segment, device, CAST(converted AS INTEGER) converted,

                          FROM gold.fct_experiment_user GROUP BY ROLLUP (device) ORDER BY device NULLS LAST")
split$device[is.na(split$device)] <- "ALL"
split$srm_p_value <- signif(mapply(function(a, b) chisq.test(c(a, b))$p.value, split$control, split$treatment), 2)

section: 20.5 Deploying in a retail or FMCG business
text:
20.5 Deploying in a retail or FMCG business

Owners: the Commercial Director (revenue, margin, promotion rules) and the Head of Trade Marketing (promo calendar, uplift method).
First 90 days: a weekly depot and category pack (the Lab dashboard); a promo post-mortem template; an experiment gate (SRM + minimum sample size) before any test is read out.
Pitfall: distributor sell-out often arrives late and is restated. Use the incremental-merge load (Chapter 6) and mark weeks as provisional until closed.

title: 20  Playbook: Retail chains and FMCG
text:
20.7 ✅ Mastery check

Why is volume uplift not the same as profit uplift for a promotion?
What is a sample-ratio mismatch (SRM), what caused it in the checkout test, and what should the business do?
How do you handle distributor sell-out that arrives late and is later restated?








Solutions






The discount gives margin away on every unit, including units customers would have bought anyway. In this data, Foods promotions sell about a third more units but gross profit barely moves. Judge promotions on gross profit uplift, and in a full analysis control for seasonality and the post-promotion dip.
An SRM means the arms are not the size the randomisation intended (here 52/48 instead of 50/50, p ≈ 0). It came almost entirely from Android: treatment users were dropped, so they are not missing at random and the naive comparison is biased. Report the clean subset with caveats (about 7% relative lift, p ≈ 0.09, not significant), fix the bug, and re-run with a sample size planned in advance before any roll-out.
Load it with the incremental-merge pattern (Chapter 6), so restated weeks replace earlier versions instead of duplicating them, and mark recent weeks provisional until the period is closed.

21.1 Decisions this platform supports
Sector Production, deferment, water cut, crude quality

title: 21  Playbook: Oil and gas (upstream)
text:
Daily production: how much did each well and asset produce versus potential, and why the gap?
Deferment: which causes cost the most barrels, and which are within our control?
Reservoir and well health: rising water cut, falling rates, wells due for intervention.
Crude quality: are samples on specification for export, by test, asset and analyst?

title: 21  Playbook: Oil and gas (upstream)
section: 21.2 Architecture mapped to upstream oil and gas
text:
21.2 Architecture mapped to upstream oil and gas







Layer
In upstream




Sources
Supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) and process historians (PI, IP.21), daily production reports (often Excel), well master (from the subsurface team), lab laboratory information management system (LIMS), maintenance (SAP PM), health, safety and environment (HSE) incident logs


Silver
Typed well-days; physically impossible values quarantined (uptime > 24 h); well master with recompletion history (slowly changing dimension, type 2 (SCD2)); downtime reasons conformed to a standard list


Gold
fct_well_day (well × day), dim_well, fct_lab_sample; marts: deferment Pareto, asset daily production report


Gate
Uptime 0–24; non-negative volumes; one row per well-day; every well in the master; asset totals reconcile to fiscal metering and allocation


Govern
Oil rate, uptime %, deferment bbl and %, water cut, gas-oil ratio, on-spec rate


Serve
06:00 daily production report (Quarto Portable Document Format (PDF)); asset dashboards; monthly regulatory returns; Dataverse for field-ops Power Apps


Plane
Production data is commercially sensitive; regulatory reporting deadlines; operational technology (OT)/information technology (IT) network separation for SCADA extracts

spec <- list(
  name = "oil_gas",
  bronze = list(production = "energy_production_daily.csv", wells = "energy_wells.csv", lab = "energy_lab_qc.csv"),
  silver = list(
    well_history = "
      SELECT well_id, asset, asset_type, CAST(spud_year AS INTEGER) spud_year, completion, artificial_lift,
             row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY well_id ORDER BY rowid) AS version,
             lead(1) OVER (PARTITION BY well_id ORDER BY rowid) IS NULL AS is_current
      FROM bronze.wells",
    well_day = "
      SELECT CAST(date AS DATE) date, well_id, asset, CAST(oil_bbl AS DOUBLE) oil_bbl, CAST(gas_volume AS DOUBLE) gas_volume,
             CAST(water_bbl AS DOUBLE) water_bbl, CAST(uptime_hrs AS DOUBLE) uptime_hrs,

      FROM bronze.production WHERE CAST(uptime_hrs AS DOUBLE) BETWEEN 0 AND 24",
    well_day_rejects = "SELECT *, 'uptime_hrs > 24' reason FROM bronze.production WHERE CAST(uptime_hrs AS DOUBLE) NOT BETWEEN 0 AND 24"),

title: 21  Playbook: Oil and gas (upstream)
text:
21.7 Deploying in an upstream operator

Owners: the Production Manager (daily report, deferment codes), Petroleum Engineering (well master), and the Lab supervisor (LIMS).
First 90 days: automate the 06:00 daily production report from the historian and the daily production report (DPR) spreadsheet, with the gate checking that asset totals reconcile to fiscal meters. Then a deferment dashboard with conformed reason codes.
Regulatory: production and reserves reporting to the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) under the Petroleum Industry Act 2021. Keep regulatory marts certified and versioned, and check current reporting templates and deadlines.
OT security: extract from the historian through a one-way interface or a demilitarised zone (DMZ) replica. The analytics platform must never be able to write to control systems.

text:
21.8 🏋️ Exercises
E21.1 🟢 Which asset has the lowest average uptime? E21.2 🟡 Compare W-007’s average daily oil rate in the six months before and after its April 2025 recompletion. Did the intervention pay off? title: 21  Playbook: Oil and gas (upstream)
text:
21.9 ✅ Mastery check

W-007 appears twice in the well master. Should you delete one row?
What belongs in the gate for daily well data?
How should the analytics platform connect to SCADA and process historians?








Solutions






No. The well was recompleted in April 2025, so this is history, not duplication. Keep both versions as a slowly changing dimension type 2 (valid-from and valid-to dates); analyses of rates before and after the recompletion need both.
Uptime between 0 and 24 hours (impossible values quarantined), non-negative volumes, one row per well-day, every well in the well master, and asset totals that reconcile to fiscal metering and allocation.
One way, read only: through a one-way interface or a replica in a demilitarised zone. The platform must never be able to write to control systems; operational technology and IT networks stay separate.

title: 22  Playbook: Power and utilities
text:
Losses: where is energy lost, technically or commercially, between receipt and cash?

title: 22  Playbook: Power and utilities
section: 22.2 Architecture mapped to a distribution company
text:
22.2 Architecture mapped to a distribution company







Layer
In power distribution




Sources
Feeder and transformer meters (advanced metering infrastructure (AMI)/meter data management (MDM), supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA)), billing system, prepaid vending, collections and bank files, customer enumeration, outage logs, field-work orders


Silver
Typed feeder-day readings; meter resets and impossible supply hours quarantined; feeders conformed to business units; customer class standardised


Gold
fct_feeder_day (feeder × day: energy received, billed, collected, supply hours); dim_feeder (band, business unit); marts: aggregate technical, commercial and collection (ATC&C) losses, band compliance


Gate
Supply hours 0–24; energy ≥ 0; billed ≤ received × tolerance; feeder in master; energy received reconciles to the Transmission Company of Nigeria (TCN)/market-operator settlement


Govern
ATC&C loss %, billing efficiency, collection efficiency, average daily supply hours, band compliance %


Serve
Executive loss dashboard; feeder league tables for business-unit managers; regulatory performance returns; Dataverse/Power Apps for field crews


Plane
Customer data (names, addresses, meter numbers) is personal; regulatory submissions certified

title: 22  Playbook: Power and utilities
text:
22.3 The key metric: ATC&C loss
Aggregate Technical, Commercial and Collection (ATC&C) loss measures how much of the energy a distributor receives never turns into cash:
\[\text{ATC\&C} = 1 - \underbrace{\frac{\text{energy billed}}{\text{energy received}}}_{\text{billing efficiency}} \times \underbrace{\frac{\text{naira collected}}{\text{naira billed}}}_{\text{collection efficiency}}\]

title: 22  Playbook: Power and utilities
text:
22.4 Data (synthetic, generated reproducibly)

set.seed(11)
bands <- c(A = 20, B = 16, C = 12, D = 8, E = 4)       # minimum average daily supply hours by band (verify current NERC order)
feeders <- data.frame(feeder_id = sprintf("FDR-%03d", 1:60),
                      business_unit = sample(c("Ikeja", "Ikorodu", "Oshodi", "Abule-Egba", "Shomolu"), 60, TRUE),
                      band = sample(names(bands), 60, TRUE, prob = c(.25, .25, .2, .15, .15)))
days <- seq(as.Date("2025-07-01"), as.Date("2025-12-31"), by = "day")
fd <- merge(feeders, data.frame(date = days))
fd$commit_h <- bands[fd$band]
fd$supply_hours <- round(pmin(24, pmax(0, rnorm(nrow(fd), fd$commit_h - ifelse(fd$band %in% c("A", "B"), 0.4, -0.2), 2.5))), 1)
fd$energy_received_mwh <- round(fd$supply_hours * runif(nrow(fd), 2.5, 4.5), 2)
fd$billing_eff <- pmin(1, rnorm(nrow(fd), ifelse(fd$band == "A", .9, .78), .05))
fd$energy_billed_mwh <- round(fd$energy_received_mwh * fd$billing_eff, 2)
fd$billed_ngn <- round(fd$energy_billed_mwh * 1000 * ifelse(fd$band == "A", 209.5, 62))   # tariffs are illustrative only
fd$collected_ngn <- round(fd$billed_ngn * pmin(1, rnorm(nrow(fd), .82, .08)))
fd$supply_hours[sample(nrow(fd), 8)] <- c(26, 31, 25.5, 48, 24.7, 30, 27, 36)            # planted: impossible hours
fd$energy_received_mwh[sample(nrow(fd), 3)] <- -999                                         # planted: meter reset
readings <- fd[, c("feeder_id", "date", "supply_hours", "energy_received_mwh", "energy_billed_mwh", "billed_ngn", "collected_ngn")]
nrow(readings)

[1] 11040

22.5 Run the pipeline

spec <- list(
  name = "power",
  bronze = list(feeders = feeders, readings = readings),
  silver = list(
    feeder_day = "SELECT feeder_id, CAST(date AS DATE) date, supply_hours, energy_received_mwh, energy_billed_mwh, billed_ngn, collected_ngn
                  FROM bronze.readings WHERE supply_hours BETWEEN 0 AND 24 AND energy_received_mwh >= 0",
    feeder_day_rejects = "SELECT *, CASE WHEN energy_received_mwh < 0 THEN 'meter reset' ELSE 'supply_hours > 24' END reason
                          FROM bronze.readings WHERE NOT (supply_hours BETWEEN 0 AND 24 AND energy_received_mwh >= 0)"),
  gold = list(
    dim_feeder = "SELECT feeder_id, business_unit, band FROM bronze.feeders",
    fct_feeder_day = "SELECT * FROM silver.feeder_day",
    mart_feeder_month = "
      SELECT f.feeder_id, f.business_unit, f.band, date_trunc('month', d.date) AS month,
             AVG(d.supply_hours) AS avg_supply_hours,
             SUM(d.energy_billed_mwh) / SUM(d.energy_received_mwh)                    AS billing_eff,
             SUM(d.collected_ngn) / SUM(d.billed_ngn)                                 AS collection_eff,
             1 - (SUM(d.energy_billed_mwh) / SUM(d.energy_received_mwh)) * (SUM(d.collected_ngn) / SUM(d.billed_ngn)) AS atcc_loss
      FROM gold.fct_feeder_day d JOIN gold.dim_feeder f USING (feeder_id) GROUP BY ALL"),

title: 22  Playbook: Power and utilities
text:
22.7 Deploying in a distribution company

Owners: the Chief Commercial Officer (billing, collection definitions) and the Chief Technical Officer (energy received, supply hours, the feeder master).
First 90 days: daily feeder readings from the MDM into the warehouse, a band-compliance league table, and an ATC&C dashboard by business unit that reconciles monthly to the market settlement.
Regulatory: Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC) tariff-band commitments and performance reporting. Confirm current band definitions and minimum hours in the latest NERC orders, and certify the compliance mart.
Pitfall: estimated billing for unmetered customers inflates billing efficiency. Tag estimated bills in silver and report metered and unmetered separately.

title: 22  Playbook: Power and utilities
text:
22.8 🏋️ Exercises
E22.1 🟢 Which business unit has the highest ATC&C loss? E22.2 🟡 List feeders that are Band A on the tariff but averaged under 20 hours in three or more months: candidates for re-banding or investment. E22.3 🔴 Estimate the naira value of reducing ATC&C by 5 points in the worst business unit, and present it as a one-page Quarto memo with a sensitivity table.

title: 22  Playbook: Power and utilities
text:
22.9 ✅ Mastery check

Define ATC&C loss and its two components. A business unit bills 80% of the energy it receives and collects 70% of what it bills: what is its loss?
Why report the band-compliance rate rather than average supply hours?
How does estimated billing distort the loss figures, and what is the fix?








Solutions






ATC&C loss \(= 1 - \text{billing efficiency} \times \text{collection efficiency}\), where billing efficiency is energy billed ÷ energy received and collection efficiency is naira collected ÷ naira billed. Here \(1 - 0.8 \times 0.7 = 0.44\): 44% of the energy received never becomes cash.
Averages hide non-compliance. Bands A and B are delivered close to their promise on average, yet many individual feeder-months fall short. Those feeders drive complaints and regulatory questions, and only a compliance rate (share of feeder-months meeting the band’s hours) shows them.
Estimated bills for unmetered customers inflate billing efficiency, making losses look smaller than they are. Tag estimated bills in silver and report metered and unmetered customers separately.

title: 23  Playbook: Financial services (banking)
text:
23.2 Architecture mapped to a bank







Layer
In banking




Sources
Core banking (Finacle, Flexcube, T24), card and channel switches, mobile/internet banking logs, customer relationship management (CRM), complaints system, NPS surveys, the Bank Verification Number (BVN)-linked customer master


Silver
One customer per real person (BVN-linked, pseudonymised); accounts and transactions typed; segments conformed; outcome-leaking fields isolated


Gold
fct_customer_month (customer × month snapshot), fct_transaction, dim_customer (slowly changing dimension, type 2 (SCD2) on segment), dim_branch; marts: churn risk, product holding, NPS drivers


Gate
Unique customer per month; balances reconcile to the general ledger; no raw BVN/National Identification Number (NIN) in gold; segment codes valid


Govern
Churn rate, active-customer definition (agreed with Finance and Risk), products per customer, digital-active %, NPS


Serve
Relationship-manager retention lists (CRM write-back via Dataverse/Dynamics); executive dashboards; certified regulatory marts


Plane
Highest sensitivity: personal and financial data; CBN and Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) obligations; strict roles; model risk management for any scoring model

Every churned customer is also flagged dormant. Either churn is defined through dormancy, or dormancy is recorded at the same time as churn. Either way, dormant cannot be used to predict churn: it is part of the outcome. The steward must document how “churn”, “dormant” and “active” relate. title: 23  Playbook: Financial services (banking)
text:
23.4 Insight: what keeps customers?

d <- dbGetQuery(bk$con, "SELECT digital_band, products_held, AVG(churned_90d) churn, COUNT(*) n FROM gold.fct_customer
                         WHERE products_held <= 5 GROUP BY ALL HAVING n > 50")
d$digital_band <- factor(d$digital_band, c("low", "mid", "high"))
ggplot(d, aes(products_held, churn, colour = digital_band)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("#E58B3C", "#7FA8D4", "#0B2C55")) +
  labs(x = "Products held", y = "90-day churn", colour = "Digital engagement", title = "More products and more digital use, less churn")









cust <- dbGetQuery(bk$con, "SELECT * FROM gold.fct_customer")
m <- glm(churned_90d ~ products_held + digital_score + salary_domiciled + complaints_12m + tenure_months + segment, binomial, cust)
round(exp(coef(m))[-1], 3)    # odds ratios: <1 protects, >1 raises churn risk

   products_held    digital_score salary_domiciled   complaints_12m 
           0.692            0.979            0.464            1.817 
   tenure_months      segmentMass   segmentPrivate       segmentSME 
           0.983            1.104            0.605            0.985 


An odds ratio below 1 means the factor is associated with lower churn. Read them as associations, not causes. Customers who domicile their salary are different in many ways. Testing a retention offer (a randomised experiment, as in the retail and pensions playbooks) is how you learn what causes customers to stay.

title: 23  Playbook: Financial services (banking)
text:
23.5 Deploying in a bank

Owners: Retail Banking (churn and active-customer definitions), Finance (balances reconciled to the general ledger (GL)), Risk (model risk management), and the data protection officer (DPO).
First 90 days: an agreed definition of active customer (the most contested number in most banks), a monthly churn dashboard reconciled to the GL, then a pilot retention list for one region’s relationship managers (RMs), with outcomes tracked.
Regulatory: CBN data and risk-management expectations; NDPA for personal data; consumer-protection rules for how retention offers are made. Customer scoring models need documentation, validation and monitoring under model risk governance.
Pitfall: BVN and account numbers leaking into analyst extracts. Pseudonymise in silver (Chapter 15), and test that no raw identifiers reach gold.

title: 23  Playbook: Financial services (banking)
text:
23.6 🏋️ Exercises
E23.1 🟢 Which branch state has the highest churn among Mass-segment customers? E23.2 🟡 Add a test that no column in gold contains values matching an 11-digit identifier pattern (Chapter 15’s scanner, as a gate test). E23.3 🔴 Design a randomised retention experiment: an offer vs control for the top-risk decile. Write the hypothesis, sample size, primary metric, guardrail metrics and the sample-ratio mismatch (SRM) check.

title: 23  Playbook: Financial services (banking)
text:
23.7 ✅ Mastery check

Why can’t the dormant flag be used to predict churn in this data?
What is wrong with an nps_last_survey column that ranges from −100 to +100 for each customer?
Customers who domicile their salary churn less (odds ratio below 1). Does domiciling salary cause retention?








Solutions






Every churned customer is also dormant. Dormancy is either part of how churn is defined or recorded at the same moment, so it is part of the outcome: the same leakage as the human resources (HR) exit-interview flag. The data steward must document how “churn”, “dormant” and “active” relate.
An individual answers 0–10; NPS is a group score (% promoters − % detractors). A −100..100 value on each customer is probably a branch or segment score copied onto every row. Averaging it again is meaningless. Ask the source owner before anyone charts it.
Not proven. It is an association: salary-domiciled customers differ in many ways. To learn what causes retention, run a randomised test of a retention offer, as in the retail and pensions playbooks.

24.2 Architecture mapped to a pension operator or regulator

24.3 Run the pipeline

spec <- list(
  name = "pensions",
  bronze = list(remittances = "pension_remittances.csv", employers = "pension_employers.csv"),
  silver = list(
    employers = "SELECT employer_code, sector, state, CAST(registered AS INTEGER) registered, CAST(employees AS INTEGER) employees, employer_name_hash FROM bronze.employers",
    remittances = "
      -- Materiality thresholds are POLICY, owned by Compliance, and passed in as parameters (see below)
      SELECT employer_code, strptime(contribution_month || '-01', '%Y-%m-%d')::DATE AS month,
             CAST(employees_reported AS INTEGER) employees_reported,
             CAST(expected_ngn AS DOUBLE) expected_ngn, CAST(remitted_ngn AS DOUBLE) remitted_ngn,
             TRY_CAST(days_late AS DOUBLE) days_late,
             CASE WHEN CAST(remitted_ngn AS DOUBLE) = 0 THEN 'unpaid'                 -- null days_late here means NOT paid, not on time
                  WHEN CAST(remitted_ngn AS DOUBLE) < 0.85 * CAST(expected_ngn AS DOUBLE) THEN 'short'
                  WHEN TRY_CAST(days_late AS DOUBLE) > 30 THEN 'late'
                  ELSE 'compliant' END AS status,
             CASE WHEN CAST(remitted_ngn AS DOUBLE) = 0 THEN 'unpaid'
                  WHEN CAST(remitted_ngn AS DOUBLE) < 0.99 * CAST(expected_ngn AS DOUBLE) THEN 'short'
                  WHEN TRY_CAST(days_late AS DOUBLE) > 0 THEN 'late'
                  ELSE 'compliant' END AS status_strict,

    fct_remittance = "SELECT *, expected_ngn - remitted_ngn AS shortfall_ngn FROM silver.remittances",
    mart_compliance = "

             AVG((r.status = 'compliant')::INT) compliance_rate, SUM(r.shortfall_ngn) shortfall_ngn,

24.5 Insight 2: do reminder letters work? (a randomised experiment)
Some employers were randomly assigned to receive a reminder letter (reminder_arm = 'letter') or nothing ('control'). Because assignment was random, the difference in subsequent default is a causal effect, unlike most of what dashboards show.

ex <- dbGetQuery(pn$con, "SELECT reminder_arm, COUNT(*) n, SUM(default_90d) AS n_default FROM gold.fct_remittance
                          WHERE reminder_arm IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1")
ex$default_rate <- round(ex$n_default / ex$n, 4)
srm_p <- chisq.test(ex$n)$p.value
pt <- prop.test(ex$n_default, ex$n)
ex; cat(sprintf("SRM check p = %.2f (balanced) | difference p = %.3g | absolute effect = %.1f percentage points",
                srm_p, pt$p.value, 100 * diff(rev(ex$default_rate))))

24.6 Insight 3: what contributors complain about
The complaint themes from Chapter 11 (vector index + clustering) belong in this platform’s gold layer. Remember the fairness lesson: an English-only keyword search under-counts the Pidgin complaints about employers deducting but not remitting. That is the very issue this regulator exists to fix.

title: 24  Playbook: Pensions (PenCom-regulated)
section: 24.7 Deploying in a pension operator or regulator
text:
24.7 Deploying in a pension operator or regulator

Owners: Compliance and Enforcement (remittance status definitions), Operations (employer register), Customer Service (complaints).
First 90 days: a reconciled monthly compliance mart; an enforcement work-queue ranked by shortfall × days unpaid; the reminder-letter experiment read-out as the first “evidence-based enforcement” story.
Regulatory: the Pension Reform Act 2014 sets employers’ remittance obligations and timelines. Encode the current deadline rule (for example, working days after salary payment) as a parameter in silver, owned by Compliance, rather than as a hard-coded number.
Pitfall: treating a null days_late as zero, which makes unpaid months look compliant. The silver rule and the warning test above exist to prevent exactly that.

title: 24  Playbook: Pensions (PenCom-regulated)
text:
24.8 🏋️ Exercises
E24.1 🟢 Which state has the largest total shortfall? E24.2 🟡 Build the enforcement work-queue: for each employer, unpaid months in the last 6 months, total shortfall, and whether a case is already open. Rank it. E24.3 🔴 Is the reminder effect the same across sectors? Estimate it by sector, and discuss why sub-group results need wider confidence intervals and pre-registration.

title: 24  Playbook: Pensions (PenCom-regulated)
text:
24.9 ✅ Mastery check

How can the same remittance data give a compliance rate of 0.2% and of about 70%? Who should choose?
Why is the reminder-letter result causal, when most dashboard findings are not?
What goes wrong if a blank days_late is treated as zero?








Solutions






They are two definitions. Strict (100% remitted ±1%, 0 days late) gives 0.2%; materiality (≥85% remitted, ≤30 days late) gives 69.8%. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions. The definition is policy, so it belongs in the semantic layer, approved by the Head of Compliance, with both thresholds as named parameters.
Employers were randomly assigned to receive a letter or not, so the groups differ only by the letter. The difference in 90-day default (29.2% vs 19.0%, about 10 percentage points, p < 0.001, with a balanced sample-ratio check) is the letter’s effect.
A blank means not yet paid, not “paid on time”. Treating it as zero makes unpaid months look compliant. Silver must distinguish the two, and a warning test watches for blanks.

25.1 Decisions this platform supports
Sector Network quality of service, site availability, customer voice

title: 25  Playbook: Telecommunications
text:
Network quality: which sites and clusters breach quality-of-service (QoS) thresholds, and why: power, transmission or capacity?
Customer experience: do complaints follow network problems, and where?
Capex prioritisation: which sites to upgrade, power or densify first?

title: 25  Playbook: Telecommunications
section: 25.2 Architecture mapped to a mobile operator
text:
25.2 Architecture mapped to a mobile operator







Layer
In telecoms




Sources
Operations support system (OSS)/network-management counters (per cell, every 15 minutes), site and power-system telemetry (generator, battery, grid), the site master, trouble tickets, customer relationship management (CRM), app-store and social reviews, call-centre notes


Silver
Counters aggregated to site-day; availability capped at 100% and impossible values quarantined; site master de-duplicated; cell-to-site mapping conformed after swaps and re-homes


Gold
fct_site_day (site × day: availability, call setup success, drop rate, traffic), dim_site (region, technology, power type); marts: QoS compliance, worst-site league; complaint themes


Gate
Rates within 0–100%; unique site-day; every site in the master; national traffic reconciles to the billing mediation volumes


Govern
Availability %, call setup success rate (CSSR), drop call rate (DCR), traffic, QoS-compliant site share, complaints per 1,000 subscribers


Serve
Network operations centre (NOC) dashboard (refreshed often); regional engineering league tables; certified QoS returns; vector search over customer reviews


Plane
Subscriber data (Mobile Station International Subscriber Directory Number (MSISDN), location) is highly sensitive and subject to NCC and Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) rules; network topology is security-sensitive

25.3 Data (synthetic network counters + the real reviews file)

set.seed(5)
sites <- data.frame(site_id = sprintf("LAG-%04d", 1:120),
                    cluster = sample(c("Lekki", "Ikeja", "Surulere", "Yaba", "Ajah", "Ikorodu"), 120, TRUE),
                    tech = sample(c("4G", "4G+5G"), 120, TRUE, prob = c(.75, .25)),
                    power = sample(c("grid+gen", "gen-only", "hybrid-solar"), 120, TRUE, prob = c(.5, .3, .2)))
sites <- rbind(sites, sites[17, ])                                   # planted: duplicate site in the master
days <- seq(as.Date("2025-10-01"), as.Date("2025-12-31"), by = "day")
k <- merge(sites[!duplicated(sites$site_id), ], data.frame(date = days))
base_av <- ifelse(k$power == "gen-only", 97.2, ifelse(k$power == "hybrid-solar", 99.3, 98.6))
k$availability_pct <- round(pmin(100, rnorm(nrow(k), base_av, 1.4)), 2)
k$cssr_pct <- round(pmin(100, rnorm(nrow(k), 98.4 + .02 * (k$availability_pct - 98), .6)), 2)
k$dcr_pct  <- round(pmax(0, rnorm(nrow(k), 1.0 + .25 * (100 - k$availability_pct), .3)), 2)
k$traffic_gb <- round(rlnorm(nrow(k), log(ifelse(k$tech == "4G+5G", 900, 450)), .3))
k$availability_pct[sample(nrow(k), 5)] <- c(104, 110.5, 101, 125, 100.4)   # planted: counter errors
counters <- k[, c("site_id", "date", "availability_pct", "cssr_pct", "dcr_pct", "traffic_gb")]
c(sites = nrow(sites), site_days = nrow(counters))

title: 25  Playbook: Telecommunications
text:
25.7 Deploying in an operator

Owners: the chief technology officer (CTO) or Network Operations (counters, site master, QoS definitions), Customer Experience (complaints), Regulatory Affairs (certified QoS returns).
First 90 days: a daily site-day QoS mart from the OSS with the gate; a worst-50-sites league table for regional engineers; then a power-to-QoS business case for hybrid conversion.
Regulatory: NCC QoS regulations define the KPIs, thresholds and measurement rules. Encode the current thresholds as parameters owned by Regulatory Affairs, and certify the QoS mart.
Scale: 15-minute counters for thousands of cells quickly reach billions of rows. Aggregate to site-hour in bronze/silver with partitioned Parquet; DuckDB handles surprisingly large volumes, and Chapter 1’s graduation triggers apply.

title: 25  Playbook: Telecommunications
text:
25.8 🏋️ Exercises
E25.1 🟢 Which cluster has the lowest QoS-compliant share? E25.2 🟡 Build a “worst 10 sites last 30 days” table, ranked by days out of compliance, with each site’s power type. E25.3 🔴 Estimate how many QoS-compliant site-days per quarter converting all gen-only sites to hybrid-solar would add, and the diesel cost saved (state your assumptions).

title: 25  Playbook: Telecommunications
text:
25.9 ✅ Mastery check

Why is site power a quality-of-service problem, and how does the platform make the case for fixing it?
What tests belong in the gate for site-day network data?
How do you cope with 15-minute counters from thousands of cells?








Solutions






When grid and generator power fail, the site goes down: availability drops and calls fail or drop. Joining power telemetry to the QoS mart shows how much each power type costs in availability, so hybrid-solar conversion can be argued in naira and in QoS terms, from the same governed numbers.
Rates within 0–100% (availability capped and impossible values quarantined), one row per site-day, every site in the site master, and national traffic that reconciles to billing mediation volumes.
Aggregate to site-hour early (in bronze and silver) and store the data as partitioned Parquet. DuckDB handles large volumes; when it no longer does, Chapter 1’s graduation triggers say when to move to a cloud warehouse.

title: 26  Capstone: prove mastery
text:
26.1 The brief
Capstone
You have built every layer once, on retail data, and seen it applied in nine sectors. The capstone asks you to do it on your own, for a sector and a decision you choose, to a standard an organisation could adopt.
You may use the course datasets, public data (Harvard Dataverse, National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)), or synthetic data you generate with documented assumptions. No real personal data.

title: 26  Capstone: prove mastery
text: Design, build and present a governed analytics platform for one decision in one organisation (real or realistic) in a sector of your choice. It must ingest at least three sources of different shapes (for example a comma-separated values (CSV) extract, a messy Excel report, and an application programming interface (API) or Dataverse table), and deliver a dashboard and one other serving target to named audiences. Everything must rebuild from raw with one command.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
Term
Meaning




Accumulating snapshot
A fact table with one row per process instance (e.g. a purchase order), updated as it moves through stages


Atomic swap
Building a new version in a temporary file and replacing the live one in one step, so readers never see a half-built state


Aggregate technical, commercial and collection (ATC&C) loss
Aggregate Technical, Commercial and Collection loss: the share of energy received by a distributor that never becomes cash


Bronze / silver / gold
The medallion layers: raw as received; cleaned and conformed; modelled for decisions


Bus matrix
A grid of business processes (facts) against shared dimensions, used to plan conformed models


Catalogue
The inventory of tables: meaning, owner, lineage, classification and test status


Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD)
Continuous integration and delivery: automatically testing and deploying every change


Conformed dimension
One dimension (e.g. dim_depot) shared by every fact that uses it, so totals agree across subject areas


Cosine similarity
A measure of how closely two vectors point in the same direction; used to compare embeddings


Common table expression (CTE)
Common table expression: a named step in a Structured Query Language (SQL) query (WITH x AS (...))


Data contract
An agreement with a source owner on format, schedule, columns and quality


Data steward
The person accountable for the meaning and quality rules of a data domain


Debounce
Waiting until an input stops changing before reacting to it, which keeps dashboards responsive


Dimension
Context for facts: who, what, where, when


Data protection impact assessment (DPIA)
Data Protection Impact Assessment: a structured review of privacy risk before high-risk processing


DuckDB
An in-process, columnar analytical database; the warehouse engine in this book


Embedding
A numeric vector representing the meaning of text (or images)


Fact
A measurement of a business event: units, naira, barrels, minutes


Fan-out
Rows multiplied by joining to a table whose key is not unique


Freshness
How recent the latest data is, relative to when it is needed


Gate
The point where tests decide whether new data is published


Grain
The precise meaning of one row in a fact table


Hierarchical navigable small world (HNSW)
Hierarchical navigable small world: an index for fast approximate nearest-neighbour search over vectors


Idempotent
Safe to run more than once with the same result


Lineage
The traceable path from a number back to its source records


Masking
Hiding part of a value (080******67) for roles that need to recognise, not read


Medallion architecture
Organising a warehouse into bronze, silver and gold layers


Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) 2023
The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, the principal data protection law in Nigeria


Parquet
A columnar, compressed, typed file format for analytics


Periodic snapshot
A fact table with one row per entity per period (e.g. depot × stock-keeping unit (SKU) × week)


Pseudonymisation
Replacing identifiers with consistent tokens that can’t be reversed without a separately held key


Quarantine
Moving rows that fail validity rules into a rejects table instead of deleting or passing them


Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
Retrieval-augmented generation: grounding an large language model (LLM)’s answer in retrieved documents


Reactive (Shiny)
A value that recomputes automatically when its inputs change


Reconciliation
Comparing totals between the warehouse and an authoritative external source


Row-level security
Restricting which rows a user can see, based on their role or attributes


Slowly changing dimension (SCD) (type 1/2)
Slowly changing dimension: overwrite history (1), or keep every version with validity dates (2)


Semantic layer
Version-controlled business definitions of metrics and dimensions, compiled to SQL for every consumer


Serving mart
A copy of gold tables shaped and placed for a particular audience or tool


Service-level agreement (SLA)
Service level agreement: e.g. “refreshed by 07:00 daily”


Sample-ratio mismatch (SRM)
Sample-ratio mismatch: an experiment’s arms are not the sizes the design intended, a sign of bias


Target leakage
Using information in a model that would not be available at prediction time


Term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF)
Term frequency × inverse document frequency: a simple word-weighting text representation


Window function
A SQL calculation across related rows that does not collapse them (running totals, ranks, lags)
